articles.title: Seattle mayor lifts pause and will expand police surveillance cameras with new safeguards
articles.author: Kurt Schlosser
paras: Seattle will expand its police surveillance camera network to three more neighborhoods, Mayor Katie Wilson said Tuesday , ending a pause she put in place in March over privacy and civil liberties concerns.

The move comes a day after NYU’s Policing Project released an independent audit of the Seattle Police Department’s Real Time Crime Center (RTCC), which Wilson commissioned during the pause. The audit found the city had built “an important foundation” for overseeing the system but that “significant policy gaps remain.” It made 19 recommendations.

Cameras in the Stadium District, installed before this summer’s FIFA World Cup, will be turned on immediately, according to the mayor’s office. Cameras around Garfield High School and in the Capitol Hill nightlife district still need to be bought and installed, which will take months. The City Council approved all three areas in 2025.

Wilson briefly turned on the 22 stadium-area cameras during the World Cup, citing “credible threats” reported by law enforcement, and said they would go off after the tournament. The audit noted that police streamed live feeds throughout the event, despite a department policy against monitoring cameras without an active call or case.

“After reviewing the evidence, the recommendations, and the safeguards available to us, I believe there is an important and responsible role for the RTCC within Seattle’s public-safety system,” Wilson said in a statement.

Wilson said the city will adopt most of the audit’s recommendations. The police department will publish a public dashboard on how the crime center is used and tighten its rules on data retention, permissible uses and requests from outside agencies. A new advisory group will help write policies for privately owned cameras, protests and where future cameras go.

The Real Time Crime Center, which launched in 2025 , pulls live video from hundreds of cameras into a single command room at police headquarters. They include 303 police-owned cameras at 61 sites, 116 security cameras at police buildings, 96 city traffic cameras, and 23 cameras owned by three local businesses that share their feeds with police.

Analysts watch 911 calls as they come in and pull up nearby cameras to give officers details callers may have missed, such as what a suspect is wearing or which way they ran. They also comb through recorded footage to help detectives investigate past crimes. The system runs on Fusus, software from Axon, the Arizona-based maker of police body cameras and Tasers.

Police are barred from using facial recognition with the system. The software does include an AI tool that searches video for people, vehicles and other objects, but analysts told auditors they use it only as a last resort because it is unreliable. In one case, a search for a man in a gray top and gray pants returned an image of a pigeon.

Whether the system reduces crime remains an open question. The Seattle Police Department has said officers and detectives are three times more likely to make an arrest with help from crime center analysts, and that the center assisted in 17 homicide cases in 2025, helping close 10. But the audit notes that the department counts any analyst action as “support,” such as checking a camera, even if it produced nothing useful.

Broader research on crime centers is thin, the audit found, and studies of surveillance cameras on their own show mixed results. A University of Pennsylvania evaluation of Seattle’s program, commissioned by the city’s inspector general, isn’t expected until late 2027.

Critics have warned that footage could end up with federal immigration agents or out-of-state prosecutors pursuing people who come to Washington for abortions or gender-affirming care. The audit found that state and city laws limit such sharing, but they can’t fully prevent it. Outside agencies could still get footage through public records requests or court orders served on the city or on Axon, which stores some of the police department’s video in its cloud.

The ACLU of Washington has previously opposed the cameras, saying they collect “a massive amount of data about people’s whereabouts” and that promised safeguards don’t guarantee the data is protected from out-of-state agencies. GeekWire has reached out to the ACLU for comment on Wilson’s decision.

Wilson said the expansion and the new safeguards go together. “We can gather evidence to hold those who commit violent acts accountable and protect our neighbors targeted by federal overreach,” she said.

Business groups praised Wilson’s decision. Jon Scholes, president and CEO of the Downtown Seattle Association, said the city “already has stringent privacy guardrails in place” and that, with police staffing “still lagging,” additional tools “are essential for solving crimes.” Lisa Howard, executive director of the Alliance for Pioneer Square, called it “a commonsense step toward making our city safer.”

City Councilmember Bob Kettle, who chairs the council’s public safety committee, said the committee will take up the audit’s recommendations, along with those from the city’s inspector general and auditor.

The city also plans to lay groundwork for connecting cameras run by Seattle Center tenants and nearby businesses to the crime center, according to the mayor’s office, citing interest from those businesses after the Bite of Seattle shooting in July. The audit flagged private camera integration as a key area to watch: the police department has bought about 100 devices that let businesses stream video to the center but hasn’t decided who will get them.

The advisory group, which will include members of the Community Police Commission, the Community Surveillance Working Group, police and other city staff, will meet over the next few months. Its recommendations will then go through the police department’s policy review process.

articles.title: Microsoft awards $20K grants to 25 Seattle-area nonprofits amid state budget crunch and tax debate
articles.author: Todd Bishop
paras: The Lighthouse for the Blind is adding braille displays to its computer lab. Friends of the Issaquah Salmon Hatchery is taking its lessons to low-income schools. And Lake Washington High School’s band boosters are replacing marching capes that date to the MS-DOS era.

Those are among 25 King County nonprofits that received $20,000 apiece from Microsoft in grants announced this week. It’s the first round of the company’s Community-First Grants, a $1 million program launched in September .
Microsoft said it received 813 applications.

“Boy, I think we hit a nerve,” said Jane Broom, Microsoft’s senior director of Community Affairs, during an event Monday recognizing the nonprofits on the company’s Redmond campus, featuring Mariners catcher Cal Raleigh and the team’s mascots.

The grants are meant for immediate needs, such as replacing a broken-down van or a failed freezer, Broom explained. Nonprofits that already received or were invited to receive Microsoft corporate grants in 2026 weren’t eligible.

Funding and the tax debate: Nonprofits are dealing with rising costs and tighter budgets. As a group, their largest funding source is the state government, which is in the middle of an ongoing debate with members of the business community over taxes and economic competitiveness amid a budget crunch.

Microsoft is among the companies asserting that current and proposed taxes are hurting the business climate. It’s also the second-largest funder of the state’s nonprofits, behind only the state itself, said Brad Smith, the company’s president and vice chair.

“In my view, a healthy nonprofit community actually has aspects of support from more than one source,” Smith said in an interview after the event, noting that state grants are often at risk when a recession forces budget cuts.

Where the money goes: Demand is climbing for many of the grant recipients. At Community Lunch on Capitol Hill , which serves free hot meals, it’s up 40% this year, and the diaper bank at Byrd Barr Place has grown from 720 families in 2021 to 1,600, Microsoft said at the event.

Friends of the Issaquah Salmon Hatchery gives more than 700 tours during the salmon season. It will use its grant to bring lessons to classrooms, mainly at Title I schools, which serve large numbers of low-income students and often can’t afford a field trip to the hatchery, said Mark Clemens, the group’s executive director.

“If they can’t bring the school to the hatchery, we will go out to the school,” said Clemens, a former Scientific American art director, who was creative director of the Modernist Cuisine cookbook project before taking over the nonprofit in 2023.

One bonus for the group, which goes by the clever acronym of FISH, was the appearance of the Mariners’ salmon mascots, which joined the group onstage for a photo op when Clemens and his colleagues accepted its grant.

The Lighthouse for the Blind, a Seattle-based nonprofit that employs blind people in manufacturing, retail and other jobs, will use its grant to upgrade its computer training lab with Windows 11 PCs, braille displays and wireless keyboards, said Antonio Rozier, the nonprofit’s IT director.

The goal is to keep employees current on screen readers and other tools so they can work alongside sighted colleagues, Rozier said. The Lighthouse also has computer labs at its three manufacturing plants, and employees can use them for personal tasks, since some don’t have that equipment at home.
Rozier called the upgraded lab “a game changer for the future.”
The Lake Washington High School Band and Jazz Boosters will buy 150 uniforms for the school’s marching band, which returned in 2025 after a 40-year absence and has been performing in capes from 1981.

Microsoft’s company culture: Most of the company’s local giving is directed by its employees. Microsoft matches their donations and adds $25 for every hour they volunteer, up to a combined $15,000 a year per person, Smith said.
That program accounts for most of the $1.9 billion that Microsoft and its employees have given to about 13,000 Washington nonprofits over the past 30 years, he said.
“We let our people decide where the money goes,” Smith said.

Microsoft’s employee base is going through a period of major change. After layoffs in July and September , the company offered voluntary buyouts last month to about 60,000 people, roughly a quarter of its global workforce. Employees have described mounting pressure to use AI, stagnant pay and a growing sense of job insecurity, The New York Times reported .
Asked about the buyouts, Smith said it’s a good time for Microsoft to keep investing in the employee experience, and he described the giving program as part of that.

Silicon Valley companies may offer more free food as a perk, he said, but Microsoft matches employee donations, giving workers who often move to the region from elsewhere a way to get involved in the community.

This year’s Microsoft Give campaign in October, the company’s biggest month for employee donations, was again a success, Smith said, showing that “employee participation and employee giving is alive and well.”
Microsoft plans to open a second round of applications for the Community-First Grants in the spring of 2027.

articles.title: Fintech giant Plaid opening Seattle engineering office, with plans to double local headcount
articles.author: Kurt Schlosser
paras: Plaid is opening an engineering office in Seattle’s Westlake neighborhood in January and plans to double its local workforce to about 80 people by next summer.

The San Francisco-based fintech company says the new 11,466-square-foot space at 1000 Dexter Ave. N. will serve as a hub for its technical teams, with most open Seattle roles focused on machine learning, data science and engineering.

Plaid said in a blog post that it chose Seattle because much of the cloud and AI technology behind modern financial infrastructure was built in the region. The company is developing AI models trained on its network to understand patterns in how money moves.

Plaid already has about 40 employees in the Seattle area, who currently work remotely, The Seattle Times reported. “There’s just great talent in Seattle, so it’s a little bit of a no-brainer for us,” Meghan Welch, Plaid’s chief people officer, told the Times.

Plaid’s careers page lists more than 50 open roles that include Seattle as a possible location, though most are also open in San Francisco, New York or other cities. About half are in data, engineering or security, with the rest spread across sales, legal, finance and other teams.

Founded in 2013, Plaid was valued at $8 billion in an employee share sale earlier this year, down from a 2021 peak of $13.4 billion. The company says more than 150 million people have used its technology to connect their financial accounts.
Plaid is led by co-founder and CEO Zachary Perret .
The new office will have views of Lake Union, an outdoor deck and event space, along with three catered meals a day, according to the company.

articles.title: Data center developers brace for new reality as election backlash sinks in
articles.author: Lisa Stiffler
paras: Data center developers already knew they had a public relations problem. This month’s midterm elections showed how much of a political problem it has become.

Voters approved data center restrictions in 44 of 45 local measures across a dozen states. Candidates who support stronger regulation of the facilities won 32 of the 34 gubernatorial races called so far. And political campaigns reportedly spent more than $380 million on TV ads referencing data centers, according to the Associated Press .
The results capped a year of accelerating resistance as tech giants plan to spend hundreds of billions of dollars on new facilities.
So what comes next? More outreach, more transparency and the expectation that states and local governments will pass data center rules, said leaders in the Pacific Northwest.

“We’ve been working and adapting our approach to meet the moment,” said John Wilson, chief financial officer of Sabey Data Centers , in an interview. “There used to be a time where we would say that our track record could speak for itself, and that’s clearly no longer the case.”
Communities nationwide have raised concerns about the facilities’ effect on rising electric bills, their water use for cooling electronics and the noise they generate.

Broader fears about artificial intelligence are also stoking the pushback, including worries that it will replace workers and appropriate human-created content, and that it can provide erroneous information, foster unhealthy relationships with users, or facilitate scams or terrorist attacks.
A renewed effort to regulate data centers is expected in January in Washington state — home to the headquarters of Sabey, Microsoft and Amazon.

Earlier this year, state Rep. Beth Doglio , D-Olympia, pushed legislation that included ratepayer protections, transparency on environmental impacts and clean energy requirements. Microsoft and the national Data Center Coalition opposed the bill, which failed.

Doglio has been meeting with stakeholders, including tech companies and data center developers, and will try again in the coming legislative session under noticeably different conditions. Fellow lawmakers, she said, will take on AI’s intersection with privacy, education, labor and other issues.
“It’s going to be a very tech-heavy session,” Doglio said.
Before voters weighed in this month, tech companies launched efforts to assuage public fears.

In January, Microsoft released its “Community First AI Infrastructure” initiative , which includes promises to pay the company’s full power costs, reject local property tax breaks, replenish more water than it uses, train local workers and fund AI education and community programs.

Last month, Amazon announced its “Built Together” program , pledging to invest $1 billion over five years in the U.S. communities where it operates data centers, including support for education and civic projects. The initiative offers similar commitments to Microsoft’s on transparency and covering its energy costs.

Wilson said Sabey also works with communities to understand and meet their needs. When a proposed campus in Indianapolis triggered significant pushback, the company brought community members to Quincy, a central Washington data center hub, to tour a Sabey facility and hear from locals about their experience.

“It requires a lot of patience. It requires a lot of transparency in our communication,” Wilson said. Sabey’s Decatur Technology Park in Indianapolis is moving ahead, and the company aims to bring it online in 2030.
But the even bigger challenge now is statewide moratoriums and data center bans — a scale of resistance that is difficult to address even when there is local support.

Oregon Gov. Tina Kotek in October directed a state agency to pause processing and issuing permits for new and expanding data centers until July 2027. Umatilla, where Sabey is developing its first Oregon campus, declared a local state of emergency over the potential loss of investment and revenue, the Oregon Capital Chronicle reported.
Even with the surge in resistance, “we’ve been able to find our way through on every project that we’ve had,” Wilson said. “I’m knocking on wood as I say that.”

Corporate commitments alone may no longer be enough to win public confidence, said Brad Smith, Microsoft vice chair and president, in a GeekWire interview. Communities increasingly want laws requiring all data center developers to build responsibly — a shift he called a “watershed” moment, “but one we anticipated.”

“[P]eople want to see everyone who builds a data center do it in a responsible way,” Smith added, “and they feel that the only way that one can obtain that result is to have some new laws that are put in place.”

Come next year, that could include Washington and impact local tech giants, Sabey and others. Baxtel , a data center industry research firm, lists 29 Microsoft facilities operating in Washington and four under construction, with Sabey operating eight facilities.

Amazon plans to build its first large-scale data centers in Washington, with proposed campuses in Walla Walla County and the Tri-Cities. Amazon did not respond to repeated requests for comment on this story.

Doglio said the next version of her bill will be more stringent. “We have to have a strong bill,” she said, adding that the public and members of her party are calling for it. Microsoft did not publicly specify which provisions triggered its opposition to the previous bill.

Wilson hopes any legislation, in Washington or elsewhere, allows flexibility and recognizes that data centers vary widely in size, impact and application. Sabey provides data center space and infrastructure for customers ranging from major cloud companies to corporations and community organizations.
“Describing all data centers as one thing is just not accurate,” Wilson said, “and it doesn’t understand the realities of the industry itself.”
Smith expressed optimism that U.S. lawmakers can find a middle ground that meets the needs of communities and tech companies.

“There’s plenty of room to draft laws that enable people to go forward and build responsible data centers without chilling the economic contributions these data centers make, especially to local communities,” he said.

articles.title: Allen Family Philanthropies gives $10M to hundreds of small arts groups across Washington state
articles.author: Kurt Schlosser
paras: Allen Family Philanthropies and Seattle nonprofit ArtsFund awarded $10 million to 745 small arts and culture organizations across Washington state, and renewed the grant program for another $10 million next year.

The latest Community Accelerator Grant awards range from $2,500 to $25,000 and reach organizations in 37 of the state’s 39 counties. The 2027 renewal brings the program’s total to $50 million over five years.
For 2026, the program focused on groups with annual budgets under $1 million, which raised the average award by about 25%, from $10,753 last year to $13,423.

The change followed a sector analysis by Allen Family Philanthropies and SMU DataArts. It found that smaller arts groups lost an average of one staff position between 2023 and 2024, while organizations with budgets over $1 million added an average of five.

“The incredible reach of this program across our state, along with the significant findings from our report, show just how much this type of flexible support is needed to bolster Washington’s rich and diverse arts and culture sector,” said Lara Littlefield, executive director of Allen Family Philanthropies.

Of this year’s grantees, 496 are in Northwest Washington, 132 in Southwest, 67 in Eastern and 50 in Central Washington. Recipients include 12 of the state’s 29 federally recognized tribes, and more than 22% are in rural counties.

A handful of the organizations blend art and technology, including Tacoma’s Fablab Nonprofit ($25,000), Seattle-based Simulated Immersive Experimental Realities ($15,000) and Bellingham Makerspace ($2,500).

The Old Hotel Art Gallery in Othello, in Adams County, has received a $25,000 grant each year since 2024. The gallery used the money to pay staff a living wage, to keep operating until its annual fundraiser, and to renovate its historic building, which now brings in rental income.
Gallery director Samantha Copas said the 2025 award “truly kept our doors open.”

Allen Family Philanthropies, formerly known as the Paul G. Allen Family Foundation, was founded in 1988 by the late Microsoft co-founder and his sister, Jody Allen. Arts and culture is one of its core program areas, along with youth and the environment. Last year the foundation committed nearly $7 million to eight Seattle Center nonprofits, including KEXP and the Museum of Pop Culture, to expand youth access to the arts.
ArtsFund will hold a virtual webinar in the spring for organizations interested in applying for 2027 grants. Details will be posted here .
See the full list of 2026 grant recipients here .

articles.title: PitchBook to give early-stage startups free access, using their data to feed a new tool for VCs
articles.author: Todd Bishop
paras: PitchBook announced a new program to give early-stage startups free use of its private-market data, if they share their financials and other company details.

The Seattle-based company says the new program, dubbed PitchBook for Startups , will feed PitchBook Origin , a new deal-sourcing product that helps venture capitalists and other investors find startups before they raise their first institutional round.

PitchBook announced both offerings Tuesday morning at Web Summit in Lisbon. Owned by Morningstar since 2016, the company has more than 3,000 employees and sells subscriptions to venture firms, private equity investors and dealmakers.

The launches come as first-time startup financings hit a record. There were an estimated 8,625 such deals in the U.S. through the third quarter, already more than the 8,507 in all of 2021, according to the PitchBook-NVCA Venture Monitor . PitchBook attributes part of the surge to AI, which it says is making it easier to start companies.

The startup program is open to pre-seed and bootstrapped companies that haven’t taken money from a venture firm or other institutional investor, or raised a priced round, the type of funding round that sets a valuation.
Founders can use PitchBook to find investors who are active in their sector and stage, and to compare their valuation and growth against similar companies.

To keep their free access, startups must update their company information every quarter. PitchBook says that information can include financials, team growth and product milestones. Only “select portions” of that data will go into Origin, the company said, without saying which.

Origin covers about 25 million companies, including stealth, pre-funding and bootstrapped companies. About 15 million of them are new to PitchBook. It scores companies on how well they match an investor’s criteria and sends alerts when they show new activity.

“What’s been missing is visibility into the stage before a company raises, when the most important signals are the hardest to see,” said Paul Santarelli, PitchBook’s chief solutions officer, in a statement announcing the products .
PitchBook didn’t disclose pricing for Origin, and the product’s web page currently asks investors to join a waitlist.

articles.title: WSDOT Seeks Feedback in I-5 High Speed Rail Survey
articles.author: Doug Trumm
paras: State officials are trying to keep the dream alive of high speed rail connecting the Cascadia region and linking Seattle, Portland, and Vancouver. The Washington State Department of Transportation (WSDOT) has a public survey open through November 13.

The survey will refine high speed rail options while also shaping the I-5 master plan the agency is putting together at the same time. Yoking together the planning for the region's primary freeway and its most promising HSR route was a conscious decision on WSDOT's part, aiming to underscore the crash course the region is on toward transportation gridlock – at least without significant intervention.

"The Cascadia megaregion is expected to grow by 3.4 million more people by 2050. This growth is equivalent to adding a city almost the size of Los Angeles to the megaregion," WSDOT noted on its project page . "The increase in population will be matched by economic growth across industries like technology, aerospace, healthcare and logistics. Recent studies show that the strain on our existing transportation system will be significant by 2050."

The survey does not provide much new information for folks who have already been engaged in this high speed rail process, which WSDOT has long been exploring – going back to a 2017 feasibility study , a 2019 business case study , and a 2020 framework study outlining a path to cross-border governmental collaboration.
WSDOT did share a project definition that sets a goal of achieving top speeds of at least 160 miles per hour.

"The purpose of the Cascadia High-Speed Rail project is to provide reliable high-speed rail service at speeds greater than 160 mph or 260 kph that is competitive with other transportation modes and improves mobility between the Cascadia megaregion’s metropolitan areas. The project purpose includes optimizing the safe and efficient movement of people in the growing Cascadia megaregion and facilitating economic development."

According to a presentation from September at the Washington Transportation Commission, the high speed rail program is spending the next year identifying "potentially feasible" route options, before spending another year refining those options.

"The Service Development Plan will be an analysis of potential routes where high speed rail could operate, an analysis of conceptual service options like the number of train trips and the number of stops that a high speed service may have," Ben Tripousis, WSDOT's Cascadia High-Speed Rail and I-5 Program Administrator told the commission. "We'll look at financing and governance as a component of the service development plan development. What the service development plan will not determine is a preferred route option or specific station locations at this time. That will be accomplished in future analysis."

WSDOT clarified that HSR would be a complement rather than a replacement for existing Amtrak Cascades service: "Cascadia High-Speed Rail would complement the existing Amtrak Cascades passenger rail service. High-speed rail would make fewer stops and travel at greater speeds than conventional rail services, likely running on new, dedicated tracks. Think of high-speed rail as the express train, while Amtrak Cascades would be the local route."

WSDOT is leading on the planning effort because 277 of the 315 miles between Portland and Vancouver, B.C. are in Washington state. That stretch could be spanned in as little as two hours with high speed rail, depending on the number of stops and the maximum speeds achieved.
In the final days of the Biden Administration, WSDOT secured a $49.7 million federal grant to fund the creation a service development plan for Cascadia high-speed rail.

WSDOT will likely be facing pressure from some quarters to widen I-5 in its master plan process. Former WSDOT secretary Roger Millar warned that widening I-5 would be prohibitively expansive and ineffective, since car traffic would swell to clog the wider artery.

High speed rail would be pricey in its own right, but with much better ability to scale up and solve the underlying problem. Unlike adding another freeway lane on I-5, high-speed rail can boost frequency to meet increased demand, rather than quickly succumbing to congestion issues and getting trapped in a cycle of induced demand .

Whether freeway expansions or light rail , large infrastructure projects are facing massive increases in construction costs, which is sure to impact high-speed rail projects as well. These cost increases are tied to a period of high inflation and sky-high costs on construction materials (linked to Trump tariffs) and fuel (tied to Trump's war in Iran). In its 2017 study, WSDOT estimated Cascadia “ultra-high speed rail” would cost between $24 billion and $42 billion — and that was before the era of high construction cost escalation hit.
A higher price tag is running headlong into a period of retreating public investment in passenger rail.

Republicans have also been pushing to overhaul grant programs funded in Biden's Infrastructure and Jobs Act to punish transit projects. Now that Democrats have retaken control of Congress, gutting transit investment seemingly should be off the agenda – although some Democrats like Washington's own Rep. Rick Larsen (who is the frontrunner to secure the coveted position of House transportation committee chair) had signed on the Republican-led legislation, which has an Orwellian name: the BUILD America 250 Act.

Meanwhile, some rail advocates have argued high speed rail has boondoggle potential – pointing to the over budget and very behind schedule California high speed rail project – as they push the state should prioritize more incremental improvements to Amtrak Cascades service that could be achieved sooner. Studies have shown high demand for conventional rail that could easily support doubling Cascades frequencies to 16 daily trips – which state lawmakers affirmed as a goal without yet allocating funding to make it happen.

Since the state is envisioning high speed rail as an express service serving fewer stops, more frequent "local" Cascades service would serve a valuable purpose once the bullet train arrives, feeding the high speed hub stations and keeping the in-between cities connected. And in the interim, it would build up a base of ridership so high speed rail can hit the ground running.

State officials are aiming to complete the high speed rail service development plan by 2028. That may put the region in position to win federal funding from a new federal administration more friendly to transit than Trump has been.

Since high speed rail will likely take more than a decade to build, its success may also require a period of political stability and continued federal commitment to infrastructure investment that the United States has not seen over the last decade. But the 2026 midterm could potentially portend a larger political shift – at least if that momentum can be sustained and cultivated.
Complete WSDOT's survey by Friday, November 13.

articles.title: King County Metro planning service changes for new Renton Transit Center
articles.author: Alex Kvenvolden
paras: As part of the Stride S1 line, Sound Transit is building a new transit center in Renton, adjacent to the existing South Renton Park and Ride. When it opens in 2028, it will be known as simply Renton Transit Center, and will replace both the existing Renton Transit Center in downtown Renton, and the adjacent South Renton Park and Ride. Commuters need not fret over lack of parking, as the new transit center will include a new garage dedicated for commuter parking that is larger than the parking at both current facilities that are reserved for transit commuters. With the transit center moving, bus service has to move with it, and Metro has made its first service proposal on what that may look like in its Renton Area Mobility Project (RAMP). Details below the jump.

King County Metro is proposing moving every route that serves the current Renton Transit Center in downtown Renton to the future Renton Transit Center. Multiple services (including both RapidRide lines) will continue to downtown Renton, but the relocated transit center will be the new transfer hub for all routes.

To move the connection point, routes 148 and 153 (which already serve the South Renton P&R before continuing to the current transit center) are going to be shortened to the new transit center (and not continue downtown). Routes 105, 240, and 907 are going to be lengthened further south to reach the new transit center. Routes 106 and 107 are going to be redirected away from downtown to the new transit center, and routes 101, 102, RapidRides F and I (current 160) lines are seeing no substantial change in routing.

Additionally, route 153 will move to operate on SW 7th St to Lind Ave in both directions, and the RapidRide F Line will move off of SW 7th, Lind Ave, and SW 16th St to run on SW Grady Way from the new Renton Transit Center to Oaksdale Ave SW. Lastly, the two Metro Flex zones serving the existing transit center will be adjusted to both cover the relocated transit center.

Service levels across most routes are going to be the same, but there are some exceptions. The most welcome change in my opinion is that route 907 will be expanded to start earlier and run later (6am to 6pm). Currently, the 907 doesn’t serve peak direction commutes at all, because historically these were covered by route 143 (e.g., northbound trips in the morning peak were all 143 trips, and after the commute is done, route 907 would start running). As a result, the last trip of the “night” on route 907 to Black Diamond from Renton TC leaves at 3:45pm (because route 143 would start covering that trip shortly after that). However, route 143 is still suspended, as it has been since 2020. Metro’s proposal will finally delete route 143 about 8 years after it was suspended, with the freed up service hours being used to expand service on route 907 and to implement the rest of the plan.

One other change in service is that short route 102 trips (which are ones that go from Seattle to S. Renton P&R, but not to Fairwood) will be converted to route 101. The same number of trips will run from Seattle to both Renton and Fairwood, but service will be simplified so that all 102 trips go to Renton TC and Fairwood, and all 101 trips will go to Renton TC and downtown Renton.

While the plan does a decent job at connecting current service to the Stride station at the new transit center, it does not provide any connections to the other Stride station in Renton at NE 44th St. I think this is a particularly unfortunate omission because parking at this station was delayed to the mid 2030s in the first realignment plan, meaning that for its first several years, the NE 44th St Station will only be useful for people going to or from walking distance of the station itself. A bus route connecting the station to the frequent route 240 a couple miles east could give local residents a way to access nearby Stride service, but as it stands, Stride service at NE 44th will be completely unusable for many local residents until the parking garage is completed.
I asked King County Metro if they had considered adding connections to NE 44th St, including a concept route that is part of their Metro Connects interim map, and I got this response:

The implementation of a new route to serve this station was not part of the scope of the Renton Area Mobility Project. As a budget-constrained project, the focus is on trying to facilitate the transit center relocation (which would require more operating resources than on the ground today, as more routes need to be extended to the new facility than there are routes that can be truncated at the new facility), without a reduction to current service levels. That task alone was challenging, and there unfortunately isn’t remaining project budget to pursue service growth at the scale of implementing a new route like [the route from Metro Connects].

While it is probably the correct decision to keep this particular project narrowly focused on the area around downtown Renton due to how many routes need to be changed in this one area and the limited amount of service hours to work with, I do hope Metro is able to secure more funding for the other station in the near future, and will evaluate potential service options whether or not they can budget additional service hours.

When I first got familiar with route 101, it was different than today. Rather than starting at South Renton P&R, then going to Renton TC, then Seattle, it actually did the Renton area “backwards”, by starting at Renton TC, then going south a bit to South Renton P&R, then going to Seattle. I always thought this was odd, because Renton TC was clearly the dominant transit hub, and also because it was going to the south park and ride before heading back north.

With south Renton being the transit hub starting in 2028, I think it makes sense to bring back the “backwards” route 101. It will save transferring riders about 10 minutes on each trip, which is quite significant!

articles.title: Seattle leaders vow to protect queer and nude history at Denny Blaine Park amid planned changes
articles.author: Justin Carder
paras: Fully clothed city leaders including Mayor Katie Wilson and Councilmember Joy Hollingsworth joined the Friends of Denny Blaine community group Monday on the drizzly shores of Lake Washington to recognize and celebrate the park and nude beach’s place in Seattle history and as “the first LGBT site on the state historic registrar in all of Washington.”

“For more than 50 years, people, LGBT people, nudists, naturists, other countercultural individuals have come to this beach, and for me, this is an opportunity to acknowledge that we matter. Our stories matter,” Jesse Miranda of Friends of Denny Blaine said Monday. “Our history matters, and our history deserves to be remembered. And the places where we found the freedom to be ourselves deserve to be.”

The event marked official historic recognition of Denny Blaine Park and its longstanding cultural significance to the local LGBTQ+ community following a long legal battle over the park and amid new efforts to create new rules and resources for the space while keeping the beach a safe — and nude — place .

“One of my favorite parts about having the opportunity to advocate for this in the way that I have has been hearing all of the stories and experiences from people about what this beach means to them and the impact it’s had on their lives,” Friends president Simon Thornton said.

Monday’s gathering took place at Denny Blaine along E Lake Washington Blvd and featured local leaders, representatives from the Seattle LGBTQ Commission , and members of Friends of Denny Blaine. Longtime community organizers also joined the afternoon ceremony to commemorate the park’s legacy.

A year ago , the Friends of Denny Blaine group celebrated the beach’s addition to the Washington Heritage Register , an “official listing of historically significant sites and properties found throughout the state” that does not have an administrative component to oversee preservation and protection of the sites.

This September , Hollingsworth led the council in passing a resolution recognizing Denny Blaine Park as a site of historical and cultural significance to Seattle’s LGBTQ+ community and establishing city support for preserving and interpreting its heritage.

The resolution included language encouraging the installation of signage reflecting the park’s historic significance and the “placement of a Pride flag or similar honorary symbol” following community engagement and departmental review — features that could be part of a planned community upgrade of the park that recognizes its legacy.

In her remarks, Hollingsworth recalled the rise of community support in 2023 as the beach’s neighbors pushed to end nudity at the park with a rushed Seattle Parks plan to install a children’s play area. Text messages later revealed then- Mayor Bruce Harrell worked with multimillionaire mall developer and Denny Blaine resident Stuart Sloan in the developer’s fight over the nude beach.

“What I heard in people’s testimony as they were talking to our Seattle Parks Department and elected officials was safety,” Hollingsworth said Monday. “But this was a safe place for them. This is where they could come and feel safe from issues that were going on in the world, stuff they might be dealing with at home, safety to meet new friends, safety to have conversations with folks, to be able to learn new things. Just that word safety, and that’s the one thing that that really stuck out to me during those moments.”

Monday’s ceremony comes as the city has held public meetings to form new guidelines for the popular nude beach after the victory in the courts against a bid from park neighbors to close the public space.

A King County Superior Court ruling in July ended a lawsuit brought by Denny Blaine Park for All , a neighbor group seeking to prohibit nudity or close the park entirely. The court ruling included directives that will shape updated rules for the park. Court-ordered mandates require a map of designated clothing-optional and required areas, accessibility initiatives, and explicit definitions distinguishing legal from illegal behavior on park grounds. Meanwhile, new features and upgrades are being planned, funded through the Park CommUNITY Fund, with a total budget of $427,000.

The park and beach are already much altered with fencing installed to separate areas of nudity from view from the street and nearby homes. Home security cameras have been installed and private security firms keep watch on the park property’s edges. Seattle Police stepped up regular patrols of the area through the long court battle and have continued to be a presence around the park.
Monday, Mayor Wilson assured the crowd that the park’s history will be protected through the changes.

“As a city, we have the responsibility to preserve these histories and to ensure that our public spaces remain places where people can gather and connect and climb that dream of belonging,” Wilson said. “Because belonging is about more than just being welcomed; it’s about ensuring that people can see themselves reflected in their communities, their institutions, and in the stories that we choose to see.”
You can learn more about the Denny Blaine Park long-term site improvement plan at engageseattleparks.com .

articles.title: ‘Evidence.com data is forever’– Audit finds Seattle Police unready for camera expansion including Capitol Hill and Central District — UPDATE: Wilson OKs expansion
articles.author: Justin Carder
paras: SPD’s CCTV map shows where the cameras are already in place and where they’re planned to be deployed

Findings from a civil rights audit of Seattle’s Real Time Crime Center challenges the Seattle Police Department’s planned camera expansion into Capitol Hill and the Central District, warning that deploying surveillance in these neighborhoods and across the city raises core constitutional risks.

Mayor Katie Wilson has said the “privacy and data governance audit” would be the basis for her next steps after her actions early this year pausing the approved expansion of the city’s Real Time Crime Center camera system over privacy concerns and worries of Seattle Police Department and federal authority overreach.
Wilson is scheduled to announce her “next steps on CCTV cameras” in an appearance with Interim SPD Chief Andre Sayles Tuesday morning at City Hall.

UPDATE 11:53 AM : Despite the concerns raised by the report, Wilson announced Tuesday that the camera system expansion will move forward, authorizing the Seattle Police Department to complete the planned expansion including Capitol Hill and the Central District. Existing cameras near the stadiums will also be turned back on immediately.
According to the announcement, the mayor is signing off on a months-long process of purchasing and installing the new cameras.

Further expansion including the Seattle Center campus where event production firms including the company behind the Capitol Hill Block Party have called for increased security surveillance , is also on the table.
Tuesday, Wilson said officials will work with the audit’s findings to address shortcomings in policy and technology.

Original report: “RTCCs and modern surveillance technologies collect information about everyone, not just criminal suspects,” the Policing Project at New York University School of Law cautions in its findings, noting that “under the new model, everyone becomes a potential subject of surveillance, regardless of whether they have done anything to attract police attention.”

CHS reported in March as Wilson followed up on campaign promises and stopped an expansion of the city’s police camera system to the stadium district, Capitol Hill’s nightlife areas, and 23rd Ave in the Central District citing concerns about how law enforcement and federal authorities might access the technology and data.
The cameras for Capitol Hill — budgeted but never installed — would cover Broadway from Capitol Hill Station to Pike/Pine and the core of the Pike/Pine nightlife zone.

In the Central District, then- Mayor Bruce Harrell and District 3 Councilmember Joy Hollingsworth pushed for the camera system to be centered around safety at Garfield High School with boundaries running from a block north of the school along E Cherry all the way to S Jackson. The western edge has been planned to include 20th Ave and the eastern edge would extend along 26th Ave.

The additions were planned to expand the SPD Real Time Crime Center surveillance camera system to include the Capitol Hill nightlife core around E Pike and Cal Anderson Park and a major swath of the Central District from E Cherry to Jackson police officials say is necessary to prevent gun violence.

The Capitol Hill system is estimated to cost around $400,000 to install and $35,000 a year to operate. The Central District installation has a budget of $425,000 and also an estimated $35,000 in “ongoing annual costs.”
In March, Wilson said SPD had yet to receive the ordered cameras from technology provider Axon .

The proposed rollout in the Central District collides with the report’s equity findings, which caution against concentrating automated police monitoring in historically marginalized and heavily policed communities.

While the initial pilot deployed 303 cameras across 61 sites in areas with higher proportions of people of color than the city average — including the Chinatown-International District, downtown, Belltown, and Aurora Ave — the audit found that SPD failed to publish the underlying data or comparative crime analyses used to justify placement decisions.
Each site is configured as a cluster of up to five cameras — typically four fixed cameras and one pan-tilt-zoom camera.

For the Central District around Garfield High School and Capitol Hill, the Policing Project urges the city to publicly disclose the crime data underlying deployment and mandate annual reassessments to verify whether conditions that justified camera installation continue to exist, ensuring cameras do not simply remain in place indefinitely.
For Capitol Hill, a frequent center for the city’s protests, the audit warns that continuous CCTV feeds threaten First Amendment rights.

According to the report, existing departmental policy requires lieutenant-level authorization before officers may record lawful demonstrations, but the findings show that RTCC cameras capture protests incidentally and continuously without triggering those required safeguards.

The audit also includes findings that private camera integrations through Axon’s “Connect Seattle” program currently operate without caps, deployment criteria, or technical masking to prevent private areas such as residential windows from being filmed. Recent reviews under the Office of Inspector General made similar findings .
Although SPD applies permanent digital masking on its own cameras, private feeds and Seattle Department of Transportation traffic cameras lack these protections.

The audit also found that technical oversight within Axon’s Fusus platform is deficient. The system does not require officers to input a case number or operational justification before viewing camera feeds.

The department also fails to log queries when analysts deploy artificial intelligence object-detection tools, a feature personnel described using only as an unreliable “last resort” after a search for a suspect in gray clothing returned an image of a pigeon.

Across both Capitol Hill and the Central District, the audit cautions against warrantless location tracking and indefinite data storage, warning that searches of camera networks allow police to retrace movements without the legal standards required under the Fourth Amendment.

The report also argues that state and municipal shield laws cannot prevent federal authorities from obtaining stored surveillance footage through administrative subpoenas or court orders served on cloud vendor Axon under the federal Stored Communications Act.

This risk is heightened by SPD’s handling of data. While raw CCTV video is deleted after five days under an internal guideline that is “not written policy, and thus could be changed at any time,” video clips and stills uploaded to Axon’s Evidence.com platform are retained indefinitely.
“Evidence.com data is forever,” SPD personnel said in one interview, according to the report.

To safeguard neighborhoods including Capitol Hill and the Central District, the report advises that Seattle require judicial warrants for retrospective tracking, end the practice of storing video evidence indefinitely, and resolve operational gaps before allowing police to access more cameras in the city.
UPDATE : The Community Not Cameras Coalition has provided a statement on the audit including this roster of key findings:
SPD keeps the video clips it saves to Evidence.com indefinitely, a practice the audit recommends ending.
The agreement that keeps Axon’s new surveillance features turned off is informal and appears nowhere in the City’s contract.
Analysts can open a camera feed without entering a case number or a reason, so no one can audit whether an analyst viewed footage for a prohibited purpose.
SPD created a case number for the World Cup and streamed live camera feeds throughout the tournament, despite its policy against watching cameras without a call for service or an active case.
The City proposed the system for gun violence, human trafficking, and persistent felony crime, and analysts may now assist with any call, including misdemeanors.
SPD did not prepare a specific analysis of where to place the cameras, and the pilot neighborhoods have a larger share of people of color than the city overall.
Real Time Crime Center staff can view 538 cameras directly, while the City describes the system as 62 .
SPD has purchased 100 devices to give to businesses at its discretion, each able to connect several private cameras to the Real Time Crime Center.
SPD applies no privacy masking to those private cameras and sets no limit on how long businesses keep the footage.

articles.title: Seattle school board authorizes court fight against Initiative 638
articles.author: Justin Carder
paras: The Seattle School Board authorized legal action challenging Initiative 638 during a special meeting Monday night. The move opens the way for the district to retain legal counsel and pursue court action over the measure which restricts transgender girls from competing in K–12 female sports and requires biological sex verification for all female student-athletes.

Seattle Public Schools Superintendent Ben Shuldiner said he would begin consultation with counsel over next steps. As superintendent, Shuldiner will be in position to shape how Seattle’s legal challenge of the initiative plays out.
The board decision comes as Washington voters are approving the restrictions with 56% of the vote. In Seattle and King County, “Yes” has been marked on only 42% of ballots.

The initiative bars transgender girls from K–12 female sports categories and mandates biological sex verification for all female student-athletes. Civil rights groups, including the Capitol Hill-based Gender Justice League , criticized the scope . “I-638 was sold as a rule about a handful of Trans youth, when in reality, it’s a medical sex check for every girl playing school sports in this state — whether Trans or not.” The ACLU of Washington said it was reviewing legal challenges.

Reaffirming its opposition first adopted in September, the board’s statement following Monday’s decision cited the measure’s inequality with restrictions centered solely on girls’ athletics, imposing scrutiny and privacy invasions not required of boys, alongside operational, financial, and administrative burdens.

“Our responsibility as a School Board is to uphold the law and protect the students and families we serve,” Board President Gina Topp said in a statement. “When a new law raises serious questions about how it interacts with existing laws and constitutional protections, we have a responsibility to seek clarity from the courts. This resolution gives the district the ability to do seek appropriate legal action so we can meet our obligations to our students.”

In the statement, Board Member-at-Large Joe Mizrahi cited conflicts with state law. “Washington has important laws that protect student privacy, guarantee equal access to educational opportunities, and ensure students are treated fairly. These laws reflect values our communities have fought for and overwhelmingly support,” Mizrahi said. “As Board Directors, we take an oath to uphold them. Right now, we don’t see a way to implement Initiative 638 without violating those vital protections. We aren’t willing to simply disregard our other legal obligations, and that’s why we’re asking the courts to help resolve this conflict.”
The resolution, the board’s statement said, reaffirmed its commitment to schools that are “safe, inclusive, affirming, and supportive for all children.”

With county and state election certifications wrapping up ahead of the measure taking effect on December 3rd, the Seattle School Board and civil rights groups will need to make emergency legal filings to halt implementation, arguing that the mandate infringes on student privacy protections and conflicts with existing state anti-discrimination statutes. Unless an injunction is granted, school districts statewide will face an early December deadline to enforce medical sex verification rules for female athletes and restructure athletic eligibility policies.

articles.title: Virgin Mirth
articles.author: Dan Savage
paras: I’m a 22-year-old male and still a virgin. I’m quite anxious about entering the dating scene because the vast majority of women my age have a lot more sexual and romantic experience and they will see my inexperience as a red flag. I also grew up with a mild case of hig h- functioning autism, so social stuff can be hard for me but I’m actively improving. I’m also living in a very rural area and most women my age have kids already, which adds to my feelings of being out of sync and undesirable . I have dealt with low self-esteem most of my life. Be honest with me: What do the majority of experienced women my age in the United States feel about 2 2 -year-old men who are virgins? Am I a huge disadvantage here? How do I talk about this with a potential partner? Any advice would be appreciated.

Your inexperience isn’t the enormous disadvantage you imagine it to be — read a newspaper — but even if it were a disadvantage, TBD, everybody’s got disadvantages: short guys, bald guys, bi guys, old guys, guys who are living in their parents’ basements. But telling yourself that no one could possibly want you because you’re short, bald, bi, etc., is the biggest disadvantage of all because it stops you from trying.

Zooming out for a second: The Kinsey Institute recently surveyed — in partnership with Playboy — thousands of young people between the ages of 18 and 29. (I discussed the results of the survey with the Kinsey Institute’s Dr. Justin Garcia on the Lovecast.) They found that fully 19% of Gen Z were virgins, TBD, with women in your age group being just as likely to report being virgins as men. Which means there are plenty of women out there close to your age, TBD, who are just as inexperienced as you are. And some of them feel just as insecure about being inexperienced as you do — they send me letters too —and while some of them might prefer an experienced partner for their first time, many would be more comfortable with someone who’s just as inexperienced. (Somebody needs to build a dating app for inexperienced people who wanna meet other inexperienced people and get laid. Call it Startr. And somebody needs to build a dating app for inexperienced people who just wanna sit at home and complain about it. Call it Martr.)

But you shouldn’t assume that experienced women couldn’t possibly be interested in you. Yes, some experienced women will pass — some of those single moms in your area won’t wanna be your first — but some won’t care and others might like the idea of breaking you in. And assuming you have other interests, ambitions, and hobbies that make you a fun hang, women who would’ve preferred an experienced partner might be willing to give your inexperienced ass a chance.

So, buck the fuck up, dude, and put yourself out there. Get on the apps, TBD, set a wide radius, and let the women you match with know you’re willing to meet for a low-stakes vibe check — just a cup of coffee — even if it means a long drive. And get the fuck out of the house: g o places , do things, meet people . Find a coffee shop or bar you like and become a regular. Join a gym and go at the same time every damn day. Find a non-profit organization in your area that’s doing something you support and volunteer. You live in the boonies: Is there a local organization out there planting trees or restoring wetlands? Grab a shovel. Even if everyone you meet planting trees is a dude, one or two of those dudes might have sisters. Or you might find yourself invited to a house party thrown by one of those dudes who — gasp — also invited friends who happen to be women. (Added perk: The more people you interact with regularly, the better you’ll get at reading social cues.)

And if you meet a girl on the apps or at a party — or when you’re out there planting trees —don’t be shy about telling her you’re new to dating and completely inexperienced with sex, TBD, because 1. that’s the truth and 2. there’s a very good chance she is, too. (Lying to someone about your experience is a red flag, being honest about your inexperience is a green flag.) If things progress and sex is on the table (or bed our couch or floor), say this to her before your clothes come off: “This is my first time — which you know, because I already told you I’m inexperienced. So, let’s go slow. Tell me what you like, tell me if I’m doing something wrong, and I’ll do the same. Deal?” And if you’re doing it at your place, make sure there are fresh sheets on your bed — and that your bed is made — and that your house is clean, TBD, especially your bathroom, and use a condom.

A lot of guys your age don’t leave the house — they don’t go places, they don’t do things, they don’t meet people — and then wonder why they’re lonely and not getting fucked. Just being the kind of guy who goes places and does things is going to give you an advantage. But don’t make the mistake of going one place, one time, and then telling yourself it was a waste because you didn’t meet someone that first time you went to the gym or planted a tree. Keep going places, keep doing things, keep meeting people.
P.S. If there really aren’t any women — single and/or childless — for a hundred miles around, TBD, consider moving to a more densely populated area if you can swing it financially.

I have been with my boyfriend for over a year and things are good. Amazing sex, we have fun together, and we agree on the important stuff. I have trust issues, to put it mildly, but I’m trying to do better. He has never given me any reason to doubt that he is faithful. Tonight we made out and I detected… an odor. I don’t know what possessed me , but I accused him of smelling like he had been eating pussy. He was shocked, assured me that he hadn’t , and said he was sad t hat I would even think that. He is considering ending things over this. I don’t blame him. He doesn’t deserve to deal with my fucked-up shit. I made an appointment with my therapist. What else can I do? I don’t want to lose this relationship. Also, on my way home I came to the realization that what I smelled was probably my own saliva on his face.
If your boyfriend had written in, GEM, I would’ve advised him to dump your ass — as much for your own sake as his.

While everyone experiences jealousy, and while assuaging a partner’s reasonable insecurities is part of the whole relationship deal, irrationally jealous people — scary jealous people — usually don’t do the work, i.e., they usually don’t get their asses into therapy, until after their jealous bullshit costs them someone they really cared about. I once dumped a guy I loved because he flew into rages when waiters smiled at me, something I had no control over, and constantly accused me of cheating on him. When he tearfully confessed that he had cheated on me — it’s always the jealous types who cheat first — he was angry that I wasn’t as angry as he thought I should be. (So, he cheated on me, but I was in trouble.) After I left him, he finally got into therapy and worked through his shit. Years later, my ex reached out to thank me for dumping him because that was the wakeup call he needed.

Now, I may be reading too much into “I don’t know what possessed me,” but my jealous ex would say the exact same thing after flying into one of his terrifying rages. You also say you have trust issues (“to put it mildly”), which is another thing my jealous ex would say after one of his rages. The problem was, he believed that his trust issues were mine to manage. (It was my job to let waiters know — using my powers of telepathy — not to smile at me?) So, my reading of your letter may be off, GEM, and you may have accused your boyfriend of having eaten someone else’s pussy moments before making out with you in a reasonable tone of voice, but given that your boyfriend is thinking about dumping you, my money is on you lost your shit and blew up at him the way my ex used to blow up at me.

Anyway, I can’t tell your boyfriend to dump you, GEM, because he didn’t write in asking for my advice. You asked for my advice and I can’t tell you to dump yourself. So, I’ll tell you this: Assuming your boyfriend doesn’t read this and dump you, you need to apologize to him profusely, GEM, without “centering yourself,” as the restorative justice kids say. (My ex’s apologies — abject and weepy and self-lacerating — were almost as bad as the rages themselves, because I would wind up having to comfort him.) You can, of course, talk about trust issues — you can’t avoid talking about them — but you have to make it clear to your boyfriend that your trust issues are your problem to solve, not his to manage, and that you will be working on them in therapy. Good luck.

articles.title: Slog AM: Washington Latinos Flip Legislative Seats for the Dems, Ranked-Choice Voting Is a Lot Like Sex, and If I Put Jimothy in the Headline You’ll Click on This
articles.author: Hunter Pauli
paras: Washington’s pasty urban press corps wasn’t paying much attention to the Yakima Valley heading into the election as a state legislative district that Democrats could flip. But they’re paying attention now. Republicans lost control for the first time in decades after the area’s Latino majority understandably turned on them. The Seattle Times has since dispatched Danny Westneat. Republicans have run Latino candidates in the region for years to account for their large vote share, which Familias Unidas por la Justicia farmworker labor organizer Edgar Franks described as “doing their own little DEI projects by trying to recruit these conservative Latinos and grooming them to be in office.”

But Trump’s ethnic cleansing campaign made the GOP brand toxic to Latinos , and the partisan swing in the 14th for Chelsea Dimas is more intense than anywhere else in the state. When Dimas first challenged Gloria Mendoza for the open House seat in the 14th in 2024, Mendoza beat her by 8 points—a blowout. Two years later, even with the incumbent advantage, Rep. Mendoza lost to Dimas by 16 points, a 23 point swing for the Democrats. Also impressive is Ezequiel Morfin’s toppling of incumbent Rep. Deb Manjarrez, who squeaked by in 2024 at 51-49 only to lose this year 41-58.
In a celebratory post , Dimas wrote that she hopes Mendoza “takes the time to reflect on the loud and clear message our working-class communidad sent this election.”

A little further to the east, one of Washington’s two remaining Republican Congressmen is throwing a temper tantrum over his fellow House members talking to the press. Rep. Michael Baumgartner managed to stay afloat during the blue wave, and, like many House reps, has never had to deal with a very robust local press corps. He’s used to media in his district publishing the statements he prepares for public consumption, and can’t stand it when reporters learn what he’s saying in private (the true self). Baumgartner has pledged not to vote for any caucus leader that speaks with Jake Sherman of Punchbowl News, an empty threat. When running for Congress in the distant past of 2012, he infamously told a reporter “go fuck yourself” in response to a pretty normal question.

You know what’s a lot like fucking? Ranked-choice voting: At least according to Alaska Dems, whose coalition by latest count has secured an effective trifecta in state government for the first time in decades. Seattle gets ranked choice voting for next year’s municipal election, requiring our local conservative activists to update their conspiracies about how Tammany Hall foreigners are stuffing the ballot boxes. Peltola is still ahead in Alaska’s US Senate race, which means Trump still says it’s rigged.

KING 5 News report on Irish crime divides local racist community: While it’s not exactly Whitey Bulger, KING 5 has been tracking the local affiliate of a nationwide construction fraud ring run by Irish nationals for months. Their latest report focused on an accused Irish fraudster who was deported by ICE but managed to get back into the country and get back to “work.” Local chuds in the social media comments are divided between modern-minded postwar racists upset the broadcaster is highlighting crime by white immigrants, and old school hibernophobic Know-Nothings fearful of evermore Catholic Democrats tipping the scales.

A Pacific Northwest senator exits the revolving door as a Palantir Man: The only real Irish Democrat power base in the Pacific Northwest sat atop the farthest reaches of the Columbia, but when the mines went so did the party influence of Butte and Anaconda. In the absence of a firm labor movement, Montana Democrats drifted into the pocket of national corporate interests rather than homegrown oligarchs, an odyssey best exemplified by former Sen. Jon Tester. Casting himself as a humble dirt farmer, Tester’s real job in DC was to set the Pentagon and CIA budget as Chairman of the Defense Appropriations Subcommittee, a job that made him many friends in the world of politics and weapons. The most right-wing Senate Democrat outside the former slave states, Tester blamed woke party branding for losing his seat in 2024 as the state party continued its collapse. He was a driving force behind the doomed scheme by state party bigwigs and rightist donors to run a Democratic candidate for Senate as an Independent, which saw the blue wave gently lap at Montana’s shores last week instead of dashing Montana Republicans on the rocks. But Tester has a new job now, shilling for Palantir . Considering that Tester for a time during the first Yemen war was the second largest Democratic recipient in the Senate of Lockheed Martin donations, his new relationship is unsurprising. He has a type.

And who was the biggest Lockheed recipient among Senate Dems back then? Why none other than Chuck Schumer, who’s angling to be Senate majority leader, but facing notable backlash from progressives given his propensity to roll over and play dead. Sen. Chris Van Hollen, who is not so deep in the pocket of weapons manufacturers and AIPAC, is knocking at Chucky’s door, Democracy Now reports .

Lockheed weapons are still killing kids in Yemen: A New York Times investigation into a recent Saudi airstrike in Yemen found a US-supplied bomb with a Lockheed Martin guidance system killed nine members of a single family, including five children, and wounded 19 others, including 13 children. In summarizing the 12 years of war the US has subjected the Yemeni people to, the Times makes a polite mistake, saying the first phase of fighting ended in 2016 when “international condemnation ultimately forced the coalition to pull back.” If only. Instead, we starved Yemen for years, oblivious to all criticism, and, like in our other wars, only ended the carnage after being defeated on the battlefield. It was Yemeni drone and missile attacks on Saudi Arabia’s oil industry that forced KSA bombers to cease their attacks, a harbinger of the large scale Ansarallah aerial counteroffensives that have crippled Saudi oil exports in this latest war.
Speaking of Yemeni air attacks on Saudi oil infrastructure, Ansarallah struck the Riyadh skyscraper headquarters of Saudi national oil company Aramco over the weekend, the BBC reports .

Boeing layoffs loom for commercial aircraft sector: The commercial air travel industry relies on cheap fuel, and the war hasn’t been good for that. It hasn’t been good for manufacturers either. Boeing announced thousands of layoffs yesterday in its commercial sector, as the company plans to build fewer planes, meaning it needs fewer employees, the Seattle Times reports . Luckily the company’s weapons division has plenty of orders that will continue to keep the Greater Seattle economy afloat.

Someone, definitely not me, wants Jimothy dead: If Boeing holds up half the sky, the other pillar of the local economy is Etsy craftsmen. Jimothy the deformed racoon has become a cash cow for local knickknack peddlers, meaning recent threats against his life as reported by KIRO 7 could have disastrous effects on local small businesses. They’re not coming for Jimothy, they’re coming for you, Jimothy’s just in the way. We can’t let him die, he’s too valuable.

Everyone in Seattle is a “socialist” until it’s time to see a three-hour Polish film about industrialization with me: SIFF finished off their Andrzej Wajda retrospective this weekend, where I (alone) caught The Promised Land , wherein a degenerated Polish nobleman, the German scion of a failed factory, and a hard-drinking Jewish speculator put aside medieval prejudice to rip off every class of person in Tsarist Łódź. articles.title: ‘The Devils’ Is Gay as Hell
articles.author: Julianne Bell
paras: Last Wednesday, I went to catch the new 4K restoration of Ken Russell’s 1971 fever dream masterpiece The Devils at SIFF Downtown.

If you’re not familiar, the film—which is adapted from Aldous Huxley’s 1952 non-fiction book The Devils of Loudun and John Whiting’s 1961 play The Devils —follows the original Hot Priest, Father Urbain Grandier (Oliver Reed), who becomes the target of witchcraft rumors for simply being too slutty. The sex-starved mother superior Sister Jeanne des Anges (Vanessa Redgrave at the top of her game) becomes fixated on Grandier, which manifests in an outbreak of hysteric “demonic possessions” among the convent’s nuns. Unsurprisingly, corrupt church and state officials try to manipulate the mayhem to their benefit by plotting Grandier’s downfall.

Russell created The Devils while questioning his own devotion to the Catholic faith, describing it as “the final nail in the coffin” of his belief. The film was met with intense controversy for its explicit depictions of sex and violence and its blasphemous themes, which earned it an X rating during its original release. The reputation stuck; in 2015, Time Out cited it as one of the “ 50 most controversial films of all time . ”Now, The Devils has gained a new audience with its 4K restoration (its rating downgraded to a mere NC-17) and has been so successful at the box office that its theatrical run has been extended multiple times.

As I snacked on SIFF Downtown’s chocolate popcorn while watching a parade of increasingly depraved acts, I was completely hypnotized by the film: the opulent glam rock-esque costumes designed by Russell’s wife Shirley, Reed and Redgrave’s staggering performances, and Peter Maxwell Davies’s haunting, discordant score, which echoes the descent into madness. I’ve never seen anything else like it. It made me feel like I had lost my mind, and I have been having flashbacks all week. I can’t wait to see it again.

One of the things that stuck out to me was how overtly GAY it was for a movie made in 1971! The film’s queer look is no accident: Genius gay icon, multi-hyphenate, and new queer cinema pioneer Derek Jarman designed the mod white sets, which were influenced by the cityscape in Fritz Lang’s Metropolis , neoclassical art, and the minimalist white backdrops in Carl Theodor Dreyer’s The Passion of Joan of Arc. (It was Jarman’s first time working in the film industry, and it took him three months to design the set, but Russell was reportedly very supportive and patient, despite his lack of speed and experience.)

The most obviously gay part of the movie is the sapphic nuns, whose repression drives them into frenzied fornication. At one point, news reaches the convent that Grandier has married a woman, spurring two of the nuns to dress up in drag as the bride and groom and conduct a mock wedding ceremony, going so far as to “consummate” the marriage on a mattress—and yes, it’s as gay as it sounds. In the film’s most famous scene, the entire cloister breaks out into a huge bacchanalian orgy, masturbating with crucifixes and grinding on a statue of Christ.

We can’t talk about this film’s queerness without discussing the flamboyant King Louis XIII, played by Graham Armitage. The film opens with a gender-ambiguous figure posed in a tableau vivant recreation of Botticelli’s The Birth of Venus, wearing nothing but gold boots and a few strategically placed gilded seashells. This is revealed to be the king, who is subsequently crowned and wrapped in flashy celestial robes—a scene that conveys the egotism of the king, the pageantry of the court, and the mockery the monarch has made of Catholicism. Later in the film, he amuses himself by shooting Protestants dressed in bird suits.

Louis XIII is far from the only character of this kind: Father Pierre Barre (Michael Gothard), a Catholic priest specializing in witch-hunting and exorcisms, is styled after the androgynous glam rock kings of the ’70s and the bowl-cutted Canon Jean Mignon, played by openly gay actor Murray Melvin, looks exactly like a modern-day twink. Also spotted: a few extras in drag and so many queer haircuts that would not look out of place on Capitol Hill today.

The Devils character I couldn’t stop thinking about was Philippe Trincant, the petulant, ringlet-curled daughter of the King’s powerful prosecutor Louis Trincant. Played by British actress Georgina Hale, she steals scene after scene with her powdered white face and green lipstick. When we first meet her, she’s lying nude and sweaty in Grandier’s bed after sex and tells him she’s pregnant, after which he unceremoniously dumps her. Later, she begs him to take her back and is spurned. Justice for Philippe!

While The Devils is a delightfully salacious, erotic piece of filmmaking, it does warrant questioning why some of its evil figures are depicted as so effeminate. On one hand, I’m disturbed by the implications of portraying queer-coded characters like King Louis XIII as villainous and vain, especially in a time that demonizes queerness so stringently. On the other, I can’t help but think of one of my favorite quotes from Carmen Maria Machado’s memoir In the Dream House :

“I think a lot about queer villains, the problem and pleasure and audacity of them. I know I should have a very specific political response to them…I should be indignant about Rebecca and Strangers on a Train and Laura and The Terror and All About Eve , and every other classic and contemporary foppish, conniving, sissy, cruel, humorless, depraved, evil, insane homosexual on the large and small screen. And yet, while I recognise the problem intellectually—the system of coding, the way villainy and queerness became a kind of shorthand for each other—I cannot help but love these fictional queer villains. I love them for all of their aesthetic lushness and theatrical glee, their fabulousness, their ruthlessness, their power. They’re always by far the most interesting characters on the screen. After all, they live in a world that hates them. They’ve adapted; they’ve learned to conceal themselves. They’ve survived.”

I couldn’t have said it better myself. Although some of these antagonists are painted, as Machado writes, as “foppish” and “cruel,” I couldn’t keep my eyes off them as they transgressed their way to the top. The Devils also makes it clear that it’s the people in power sowing and reaping the rewards of moral panic who are the real villains—an all-too-familiar message for our times—and the campy pageantry and theatrics make it a cinematic feast well worth its 144-minute runtime. There are still some showtimes available at Regal Meridian before it closes on Wednesday, so see it while you can!
