articles.title: Democrats’ agenda will be set by their ability to organize and compromise — not by the socialist, progressive or centrist factions all claiming victory
articles.author:
<name>SoRelle Wyckoff Gaynor, Assistant Professor of Public Policy and Politics, University of Virginia</name>
      <foaf:homepage rdf:resource="https://theconversation.com/profiles/sorelle-wyckoff-gaynor-2532648"/>
paras: The massive Democratic majority in the U.S. House and Senate that was ushered in by a historic blue midterm vote is an ideologically diverse one .

Candidates spent much of the past year differentiating their positions from the mainstream Democratic coalition. The result is a freshman class filled with as many progressive liberals as moderate problem solvers .

By the morning after Election Day, pundits and current Democratic members across the political spectrum were quick to claim their ideologically aligned candidates as the “ majority makers ” – the group most responsible for the large victory.
Centrist Democrats pointed to pragmatic moderates flipping Trump-won seats. Liberal voices highlighted the enthusiasm and turnout driven by a new, progressive vision.
As a result, days after the election the focus had turned toward January: Who will become the majority maker within Congress?

Party caucus leaders have already started building their roster : The Progressive Caucus claims at least 25 new members in their ranks, growing their membership to over 100 Democratic members. The moderate Blue Dog Caucus doubled in size , from 10 to 20 new members. And in the middle, the center-left New Dems are projecting a caucus of over 140 members.

I’m a political scientist who has worked in and now studies Congress . Figuring out the dynamics and direction of the 120th Congress requires looking at more than the ideological positions of the candidates who won. Instead, focusing on the number of candidates who won can provide insight into the direction of the party as a whole.

The large – and at the time of writing, still growing – margins of Democratic control in the 120th Congress are the biggest since 1993 , before Congress became consistently competitive and increasingly polarized. Those large margins provide essential context for understanding how this new ideological coalition will work in Congress.

While history demonstrates that an ideologically diverse party can be hard to wrangle , the size of the new Democratic majority provides some breathing room for policy negotiation and procedural debates.

Unlike the current Republican Caucus that is reliant on keeping historically narrow majorities together to pass party goals, future Democratic leadership can stand to lose a few votes. With a minimum of 254 seats in the House and 54 seats in the Senate , small-scale Democratic defections are irrelevant.
This breathing room provides the potential for negotiation, while also limiting any mandate an ideological group may claim.

For instance, the 120th Congress will have eight members in the House who are backed or affiliated with the Democratic Socialists of America , known as the DSA. In raw terms of political power, when the majority has at least 36 votes to spare on any given party-line bill, this group may not matter in policymaking.

If a group – say, the entirety of the Progressive Caucus’ 100-plus membership – decides to stick together, leadership will be forced to listen. Thus, the potential power of ideological factions depends not only on their ideas but their own organizational skills.

When groups in Congress develop practices such as confidential meetings or binding rules that require members vote together on certain votes, the legitimacy of group demands can be strengthened. This is a strategy that has been employed with relative success by the far-right Republican Freedom Caucus since it was formed in 2014.
The overarching policy goals for newly elected Democrats are consistent across the ideological spectrum: lowering the cost of living and rooting out corruption.

This was highlighted in acceptance speeches by Democrats from South Carolina to Texas to Michigan . All emphasized the same policy-focused promise: Instead of fighting left versus right, the fight should focus on the top versus the bottom.
This shared vision is no doubt important. My research has shown that a cohesive message is a key part of winning and maintaining majority control.

However, the “blue tsunami” was powered by voters with very specific policy demands. And as is always the case with policymaking, the details matter. Does healthcare reform mean reinstating the Obamacare subsidies set to expire on Jan. 1, 2027? Or does it mean something bolder, such as Medicare for All ?
While there is power in numbers, the organizational strength and ultimate success of ideological groups in Congress depends on how unified they can be around specific policy goals and proposals.
This means that who is doing the unifying also matters.
The success of any potential legislative package heavily relies on congressional leaders’ knowledge of congressional rules and their willingness to incorporate member viewpoints.

This necessity of having leadership in place to get legislation moving is epitomized by the order of operations for a new congressional session. In the coming weeks, both parties will hold closed-door, secret-ballot elections to select their new party leaders . That’s well before any legislation is even drafted.

With a Democratic caucus filled with anti-establishment candidates across the ideological spectrum, and external pressure from political pundits to dump current Democratic leadership , the future of the Democratic Party has been projected onto this otherwise ritualistic vote .

But the power and success of congressional leadership lies in its procedural acumen, not its ideological vision. Some already in Congress have noted New York Democratic Rep. Hakeem Jeffries’ experience and working relationships in discussions of whether he should be house speaker. Furthermore, groups can extract concessions during leadership selection in exchange for their support, such as seats on powerful committees or an agreement on policy agenda items.

Sen. Chuck Schumer, the longtime New York lawmaker aiming to lead Senate Democrats again, faces more public criticism from his party . While no one has yet stepped up as an alternative, momentum is building for Maryland Sen. Chris Van Hollen , who has said he is “in listening mode.”

To external observers, the selection of party leadership seems like a defining point for the party. But whether a new caucus translates to new leaders or new rules ultimately depends on the organizational power of new members and their already-serving co-workers – and what a party leader can offer them in terms of policy goals and procedural capabilities. Who is chosen as leader is not necessarily a signal of what the party’s policy goals will be.

That picture is not yet clear – and it may not be for some time. After all, the new Democratic margins in Congress are a result of a collection of majority makers. The margins of victory tell a story about more than presidential backlash. Across the country, progressive enthusiasm and moderate appeal turned voters toward the Democratic Party . And while everything is local, national enthusiasm matters, too.

The 120th Congress will include progressives and moderates and the establishment candidates in the middle that are all required parts of the same whole. Or as political scientist E.E. Schattschneider argued in 1960 in his seminal work “ The Semisovereign People ,” it would be a mistake to give credit to one group for the success of an election. Rather, achieving a consequential majority in America requires coalition building – and maintenance.

articles.title: After midterm rout, Republicans can still confirm a Supreme Court justice, but at what cost?
articles.author:
<name>Paul M. Collins Jr., Professor of Legal Studies and Political Science, UMass Amherst</name>
      <foaf:homepage rdf:resource="https://theconversation.com/profiles/paul-m-collins-jr-241509"/>
paras: The 2026 midterm rout that awarded Democrats decisive majorities in the Senate and House has also sparked interest in the future of the U.S. Supreme Court .

With Democrats securing at least a 54-seat majority in the Senate on Jan. 3, 2027 , the window is rapidly closing for President Donald Trump to appoint a new Supreme Court justice and safeguard conservative dominance on the court for decades.

As a Supreme Court scholar , I know that judicial appointments have real consequences. Look no further than Roe v. Wade : Within two years of securing a 6–3 conservative majority, the high court in 2022 eliminated the constitutional right to abortion that had existed for almost 50 years.
Now that Democrats have taken the Senate, if a Republican-appointed justice retires before Jan. 3, it will trigger one of the most explosive confirmation battles in American history.
Here’s how the fight is likely to play out – and why the stakes are so high.

Justices Samuel Alito and Clarence Thomas top the list of potential retirees after Democrats won the Senate – even if Alito has reportedly said he will not retire immediately . Alito and Thomas are the court’s oldest justices, at 76 and 78, respectively. Thomas is the court’s longest-serving justice, appointed by President George H.W. Bush in 1991.

Perhaps more importantly, both justices have deep ties to the conservative legal movement . This is a network of lawyers, judges and politicians who seek to etch conservative principles into law. Overturning Roe v. Wade was at the top of the conservative wish list .
My research suggests that both Alito and Thomas care about their legacies . And they both understand that a Democratic-controlled Senate will block another Trump-appointed nominee.

Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer made this clear just days after the midterms. And in October 2026, Senate Judiciary Committee member Richard Blumenthal, the Democrat from Connecticut , said, “It is slim to none that we would support a nominee from this administration.”
Though Alito has indicated he intends to stay on the court through its 2026 term, Thomas has made no recent public statements about retirement. And Alito is free to change his mind at any time.

If Alito or Thomas announce their retirement soon, Republicans would have enough time to confirm a successor. The Senate has four and a half work weeks scheduled between Election Day and Jan. 3. Justice Amy Coney Barrett was confirmed less than a month after her nomination, making the timeline tight but doable.

Democrats will likely attempt to slow down the process, but they face an uphill battle with few options. Republicans stripped away key delaying tactics in recent years by ending the filibuster in 2017 and ignoring the Judiciary Committee’s quorum rules in 2020. This rule requires nine members be present to transact business, including two members of the minority party.
A Republican effort to confirm a Supreme Court nominee during a lame-duck Senate would spark a historic battle with Democrats.

Democrats would surely point to how Republicans handled President Barack Obama’s appointment of Merrick Garland in 2016. A seat on the court opened up after conservative Antonin Scalia died on Feb. 13, almost nine months before the November presidential election.

Republicans refused to move Garland’s nomination through the confirmation process, using their majority power to set the Senate’s agenda . This marked the first time since 1866 that a Supreme Court nomination that was not withdrawn failed to receive an up-or-down vote in the Senate.

To justify this, Republicans created the so-called “ McConnell Rule ,” named after former Senate Majority Leader Mitch McConnell of Kentucky. According to McConnell , the Senate should not fill Supreme Court vacancies “in the middle of a presidential election year.”
Four years later, Senate Republicans abruptly abandoned the rule . This allowed them to push through Coney Barrett’s confirmation just days before the 2020 presidential election.
Democrats did not take kindly to this reversal.
Schumer pulled no punches in a speech the day of Barrett’s confirmation vote. Schumer said the day “will go down as one of the darkest days in the 231-year history of the United States Senate.”

He alleged the Republican majority made “a mockery of its own stated principle – that the American people deserve a voice in the selection of Supreme Court Justices – completing the partisan theft of two seats on the Supreme Court using completely contradictory rationales.”
Democrats were clearly outraged by what they saw as two stolen Supreme Court seats.
However, I believe that pushing through a nominee will trigger an even fiercer fight. Senate Democrats will see such a confirmation as a power grab that sidelines the voice of voters.
Furthermore, if a Republican justice retires after the midterms, the move will almost certainly be viewed as purely partisan.

This has the potential to further erode public support for the court , which is sitting near historic lows . And it will likely fuel the fire of Supreme Court reform, including the possibility of expanding the number of justices on the court .
Put simply, in securing a short-term conservative victory, Republicans may end up handing Democrats the exact justification they need to reshape the high court.
This is an updated version of an article originally published on Oct. 14, 2026 .

articles.title: US national debt keeps rising after years of tax cuts – and this will make policymaking all the more difficult
articles.author:
<name>Hinckley Jones-Sanpei, Public Policy Researcher, University of Denver</name>
      <foaf:homepage rdf:resource="https://theconversation.com/profiles/hinckley-jones-sanpei-1471458"/>
paras: Democrats, set to take over Congress with robust majorities, will face at least one expensive obstacle to their policy agenda: a national debt that now equals the size of the U.S. economy.

Clocking in at US$32 trillion, this debt-to-GDP ratio of 100% would likely raise alarms for other countries. But it attracted relatively little attention in an election season dominated by concerns over the economy and the cost of living .

Debt has grown to these levels because over the past 25 years, the federal government has been spending more than it collects in taxes . Even as the U.S. economy grew, lawmakers have cut taxes repeatedly, sometimes with bipartisan support, instead of paying down debt.

The series of tax cuts since 2001 has added over $10 trillion to the debt, according to an analysis of Congressional Budget Office data by the Center for American Progress. In fact, without these series of cuts, the debt-to-GDP ratio would be decreasing, the study found.

The debate over taxation often falls along partisan lines, with arguments focusing on which income groups are affected or the potential impact on economic growth. But as a public policy scholar , I believe that important context is often overlooked. Under conditions of strong gross domestic product growth and low debt, tax cuts may have a relatively benign fiscal impact . But today, because debt as a share of GDP is so much higher, and interest rates are steeper , the cost of adding new debt is much greater than 15 or 20 years ago, whether through additional spending or through tax cuts.
I believe Democrats will have to wrestle with this math as they try to advance a policy agenda focused on affordability that minimizes the risk of further borrowing.
Proponents of fiscal austerity argue that lower spending should accompany tax cuts so that debt doesn’t rise.
U.S. federal spending, however, has remained relatively flat – outside of emergencies like the 2009 recovery package and COVID-19 stimulus funds – even as GDP has risen.

At the same time, each round of tax cuts over the past quarter century has actually gotten smaller over time if they’re assessed as a share of GDP, as a study by the Tax Foundation , a nonpartisan think tank, noted.

President Ronald Reagan’s 1981 tax cuts were the most expensive in history, reducing annual federal revenue on average by 2.9% of GDP, according to the Tax Foundation’s analysis . The next two biggest cuts occurred in 1945 and 1948, when the government rolled back the wartime hikes that helped pay for World War II. President Barack Obama’s 2012 legislation, extending most of the temporary tax cuts passed under President George W. Bush, comes in fourth at 1.8% of GDP, while cuts passed under President Lyndon Johnson in 1964 rank fifth.
Coming in sixth place at 1.2% of GDP: President Donald Trump’s sweeping policy and tax legislation in 2025, which made permanent most of his 2017 tax cuts.

While the Trump cuts amounted to a relatively small share of GDP, they had a much larger effect on the national debt due in part to the higher cost of borrowing. The original 2017 legislation was projected to increase public debt from 91.2% to 97.1% of GDP by 2027, with an overall 10-year cost of $1.5 trillion . That was based on the assumption the cuts would expire after 2025.

But just like the earlier round of Bush tax cuts, Congress was loathe to let those provisions lapse. In 2025, the narrow Republican majority pushed through Trump’s legislation that extended or made permanent the 2017 cuts.

The Congressional Budget Office, the independent government scorekeeper of legislation, estimated that the 2025 bill would add another $3.4 trillion over 10 years. And it projected that increasing deficits would push debt to 116% of GDP by the end of 2034 .
A basic calculation explains when debt stays stable, and when it does not.

If a government runs a “primary” budget surplus – that is, excluding interest payments – and economic growth is higher than the interest rate on government bonds, debt remains stable . The problem for the U.S. is that budget deficits have been growing faster than the economy, while interest payments on government debt are rising as well.

This math explains why the trajectory of economic growth is so important in understanding the impact of tax cuts. When taxes were cut after World War II, the economy was booming, the U.S. carried little debt, and reducing taxes didn’t further add to it. By contrast, government spending ballooned under Reagan, thanks in large part to defense outlays. Combined with lower tax revenue due to tax cuts , the national debt tripled during Reagan’s time in office.

In 2000, the economy was surging again. That was the last time the U.S. took in more tax revenue than it spent and began paying down the debt. President George W. Bush cited this surplus to justify his first round of major tax cuts in 2001, which also drew support from some Democrats.

It remains to be seen how much leverage the results of the midterms will grant Democratic lawmakers in the next two years as they try to enact legislation under Trump. But I believe lawmakers of all stripes will have to confront the hard choices that the U.S. national debt imposes on policy directions going ahead, thanks to a long series of decisions made over the past quarter century.

articles.title: When a Walmart closes, what happens to nearby stores?
articles.author:
<name>Vivek Astvansh, Associate Professor of Quantitative Marketing and Computational Data Science, Binghamton University, State University of New York</name>
      <foaf:homepage rdf:resource="https://theconversation.com/profiles/vivek-astvansh-1318943"/>
paras: Shoppers often greet the closure of a Walmart with dismay , while competitors find cause to celebrate.
Among critics of the big-box behemoth, a long-held assumption is that once a Walmart disappears, shoppers seeking groceries, household goods, meals and services will flow to businesses down the road.
But what if the economic downside of a closure is bigger?

We are marketing scholars who have studied dozens of Walmart closures in the United States. We found that nearby stores saw a slump in both monthly shopper traffic and sales revenue by roughly a quarter in contrast to comparable stores near Walmart locations that remained open. Our sample covered 39 Walmart stores that closed across 20 states from 2019 to 2026.

This finding suggests a large retailer can play two roles at once. Walmart competes with neighboring businesses for shopper visits and spending. But it can also act as an anchor, giving people a reason to travel to a shopping area in the first place. When that anchor disappears, the loss of shared shopper traffic can outweigh the benefit of having one less competitor.

Our finding underscores that retailers don’t operate as isolated dots on a map. Shoppers often decide where to go before deciding which stores they’ll visit once they get there. A trip to Walmart can generate a stop at a nearby restaurant, pharmacy, salon, specialty retailer or service business.

Economists call this kind of benefit an agglomeration effect : Businesses can gain from being near other businesses because the location itself attracts shoppers. Shopping center owners have long recognized this logic by using prominent stores to anchor a mix of tenants.

Other researchers have found that Walmart’s entry into a shopping area causes sales in nearby existing stores to drop . But these shops can adjust their product assortment, prices and promotions to mitigate this effect, follow-up studies suggest . What has not been studied until now is what happens when a Walmart store – or any other anchor store – closes.

A Walmart closure creates a tug-of-war between two forces, we argue. Competitive relief helps nearby businesses because a formidable rival is gone. But agglomeration loss hurts them because fewer shoppers have a reason to visit the area.
This means a store can capture a larger share of local consumer demand after Walmart leaves and still end up worse off if the total pool of shoppers arriving in the area shrinks enough.

We combined closure dates with monthly store-level shopper traffic and spending data. For each closed Walmart, we identified nearby non-Walmart businesses and compared their post-closure performance with that of businesses near Walmarts that stayed open.

We discovered not just a sizable decline in both shopper traffic and sales revenue after closure but a worsening trend in both over time. Specifically, following a Walmart’s closure, nearby stores experienced a roughly 5% drop in the following month and 6% in the month thereafter. The decline keeps getting worse, reaching about 17% in the ninth month and 20% a year after the anchor store closes.

That parallel movement in traffic and sales matters. If nearby stores were simply selling less to the same number of shoppers, we would expect spending per visit to fall. Instead, what was also happening is that fewer shoppers visited nearby businesses after the anchor disappeared.
In short, competitive relief didn’t overcome the loss of traffic that would have been generated by trips to the anchor store. But not all nearby businesses were affected equally.

Stores that competed more directly with Walmart had better post-closure sales than noncompeting stores. That is what we would expect if competitive relief is real: Grocery stores and other close substitutes are better positioned to capture some of the displaced consumer demand.

Well-known brand stores also fared relatively better than unbranded businesses. A recognizable brand can give shoppers an independent reason to visit, reducing reliance on traffic generated by the nearby anchor. And stores surrounded by more outlets with its own brands also had more favorable post-closure sales.

Another important factor is digital reach. Not surprisingly, the more a business engages with customers online, the less it depends on people physically traveling to a cluster of stores. We found that stores with a higher share of revenue from online orders saw a less severe drop in sales after a Walmart closed.
These patterns suggest that managers have options and can act: Opening another location or expanding online sales can protect a retailer from an anchor closure.

A large retailer decides whether to keep a store open based primarily on what makes sense for its own portfolio. But the surrounding businesses face a different calculation. A location that looks weak from the anchor retailer’s perspective can still drive valuable traffic to neighboring stores.

That creates what economists call an externality – a positive or negative effect of an economic activity that impacts other parties even though market prices don’t reflect it. In this case, some of the economic value produced by an anchor sits outside the anchor’s own sales and profits.

For neighboring businesses, the lesson is not to assume that a powerful competitor’s departure will create a windfall. Rather, managers need to know how many customers arrive because of the broader shopping destination, not merely how much their store’s products overlap with the anchor’s.

Meanwhile, commercial property owners should treat losing an anchor as more than risking an empty storefront. It can also hurt the rest of their portfolio by reducing consumer demand. Replacing the tenant quickly matters, but so does finding a replacement that can generate trips to the area.

Finally, local governments and economic development organizations need to understand that a major retail closure may affect businesses with no contractual relationship to the closed store. So their responses should extend beyond the vacant property itself – whether it’s speeding redevelopment, coordinating with local businesses and property owners to improve shoppers’ access, or helping create a new destination that restores shopper traffic.

articles.title: COP31: Governments are failing to rein in emissions from their own power plants
articles.author:
<name>Don Grant, Professor of Sociology, University of Colorado Boulder</name>
      <foaf:homepage rdf:resource="https://theconversation.com/profiles/don-grant-2717182"/>
paras: World leaders meeting at the annual U.N. climate summit in November 2026 are wrestling with a persistent challenge: how to get countries to follow through on their commitments to reduce greenhouse gas emissions that are warming the planet.

One of the biggest problems has long been fossil fuel power plants, but new research shows that one type of power plant in particular has been slowest to change: those owned by the very governments making the promises and writing the laws.

My colleagues and I examined carbon dioxide emissions from thousands of fossil-fueled power plants across 134 countries. What we found reveals an important hurdle to achieving the world’s goals for keeping climate change in check.

Although countries have adopted a variety of pricing, regulatory and subsidy measures designed to curb the emissions of the electricity sector, the effectiveness of these climate policies depends on utilities responding to them .

We found that power plants owned by governments had the highest emissions as a group and didn’t cut their emissions as quickly as investor-owned facilities did in response to most policies. That does not necessarily mean they are violating policy requirements, but they were slower to move.
This matters because governments control nearly two-thirds of the world’s electricity-generating capacity .

The results suggest that to limit global warming, governments need to do more than just enact climate policies – they need to ensure that all plants translate those policies into meaningful emissions cuts.
Of the 13,661 power plants that my colleagues Minh Anh Ly and Musabber Ali Chisty and I studied, 5,149 were government-owned – about 38% of them.

But those government-owned plants were responsible for 69% of the carbon emissions , based on the plants we reviewed. Together, power plants are the largest source of climate-warming carbon pollution globally .

On average, we found that government-owned power plants emitted roughly 910,000 metric tons of carbon dioxide annually – three times the average of 290,000 tons for investor-owned plants and over eight times the average of 109,000 for cooperatively owned plants.
Part of the reason for the difference is that governments often invest in large power plants that burn the dirtiest fuel – coal .

However, we also compared the plants’ emissions in 2018 to their emissions a decade earlier and looked at different national policies that were applied over that time. We found some interesting results.
Several policies were statistically associated with investor-owned power plants cutting their emissions from 2009 to 2018, including:
Pricing policies such as carbon taxes that charge companies for emissions released and emission trading systems that set limits that tighten over time.
Fossil fuel subsidy reforms that cut federal support for using fossil fuels.
Regulation policies like air pollution standards and banning and phasing out coal plants.
Renewable portfolio standards that require utilities to expand their use of renewable energy.
Subsidy policies that increase renewable energy use.
But when it came to government-owned power plants, only renewable portfolio standards were associated with significant emissions cuts. The other policies had little effect on their emissions.
These differences also appeared when we examined the stringency of policies, meaning how demanding the policy is, and the amount of time utilities have had to adjust to the policies.
So, what might explain why government-owned utilities respond differently?

Government ownership creates competing pressures that other plants are less subject to. For example, state-owned utilities may be expected to provide affordable electricity, support job growth and generate tax revenue for governments. In countries dependent on payments from companies that extract fossil fuels, utilities may also face political pressure to keep coal and gas facilities operating .

South Africa’s state-owned utility, Eskom, is a prime example. It runs a fleet of aging coal-fired power plants that make it the country’s biggest polluter. But it also provides about 90% of South Africa’s power , and when the country has faced power shortages , it has at times violated emissions standards. Despite years of climate talks, Eskom’s emissions fell little in the 2010s . They have fallen about 16% since 2019 , in part due to power outages and more people relying on home solar.

The extra pressure may make it harder for government-owned power plants to reduce their emissions than for private utilities that are accountable to fewer stakeholders and can respond more directly to financial incentives to shift toward cleaner production.

There is also a potential conflict when the same government both regulates and owns a utility. Officials may be reluctant to impose costs that could raise electricity prices or require public subsidies. Our study did not measure enforcement, so we couldn’t establish that publicly owned facilities receive special treatment or disregard legal requirements.

Our findings suggest that in addition to persuading governments to adopt and enforce more ambitious climate policies, negotiators at the U.N. climate talks will need to get governments to ensure that the power plants they own actually respond to those policies.
Here are three ways governments could do more to get their own power plants to cut emissions.

Governments could follow the example of Ireland and establish emissions-reductions targets specifically for publicly owned utilities and tie managers’ performance reviews, investment approvals and public reporting to measurable progress. Targets are more likely to get attention when managers are held accountable for meeting them. Ireland’s emissions from electricity production fell by more than a quarter from 2019, when it added emissions-reduction targets, to 2025.

They could also do more to address the financial and political constraints their utilities face. In Morocco, for example, international financing helped a state-owned agency expand solar power while limiting costs to electricity consumers. Similar measures, combined with assistance for communities affected by coal-plant closures, could make emissions reductions more feasible.

And governments could pay closer attention to emissions of individual plants as opposed to power sectors as a whole. Publishing comparable annual plant-level emissions and flagging facilities with persistently high pollution would reveal whether sector-wide gains are masking a lack of progress at specific plants.

None of this is to suggest that privatization is the answer to climate change. Government-owned power plants offer special advantages, like coordinating long-term investment and providing reliable electricity in underserved areas. The data shows, however, that for governments to meet their obligations, they need to look closely at their own plants’ emissions, as well.
Don Grant received funding from the National Science Foundation (award # 1824106).

articles.title: Economic coercion once ousted Iran’s leader – but that was the 1950s; don’t expect a repeat today
articles.author:
<name>Eric Lob, Associate Professor of Politics and International Relations, Florida International University</name>
      <foaf:homepage rdf:resource="https://theconversation.com/profiles/eric-lob-1479664"/>
paras: “Very little gets into, or out of, Iran!” President Donald Trump claimed on Nov. 8, 2026, in a social media post that also lauded “history’s greatest Naval Blockade.”

It followed the unveiling of Task Force Iron Gate – the Trump administration’s latest plan to isolate the Iranian economy in a bid to coerce the government in Tehran to bend to Washington’s will. At the same time, Trump has suggested that a return to open war with Iran is “highly unlikely.”

From my perspective as an expert on Iran’s relations with the wider world, I believe that the U.S. war in Iran – now into its ninth month – is increasingly resembling an earlier episode of Iranian-Western conflict. In the early 1950s, the British imposed a two-year blockade and embargo against Iran after Iran’s then-prime minister, Mohammad Mossadegh, nationalized the country’s U.K.-controlled oil industry.
These efforts culminated in a 1953 British- and American-backed plot to stir up protest in Iran and eventually overthrow Mossadegh .

Seventy-three years later, many of those themes – oil, economic coercion, political intervention – ring true again. Trump’s stated and shifting justifications for the war include imminent threat preemption and nuclear nonproliferation. Yet his main motivations seem to be choosing Iran’s leader and controlling its oil .

Having failed to achieve this through direct military force, Trump’s main means for achieving the objectives are now a naval blockade and economic isolation – much like the British some seven decades earlier.

But there the analogy may end. Unlike during the Mossadegh era, Iran has shown it can fight back against foreign intervention and coercive economic actions through asymmetric warfare and economic disruption.

In March 1951, one month before becoming prime minister and while serving as a parliamentary representative, Mossadegh persuaded the Iranian parliament to pass legislation that nationalized the Anglo-Iranian Oil Company. While popular with many Iranians, who perceived it as a long overdue measure to reclaim the nation’s independence and control its wealth, the move was considered by the British a breach of contract and a theft of its largest overseas asset.

The U.K. filed complaints with the newly created United Nations Security Council . But in July of that year, negotiations stalled and tensions escalated between Mossadegh – now the prime minister – and the British.

Economic coercion began with the British obstructing Iran’s oil sales by informing Iranian tankers that their receipts – issued when cargo is loaded on board – would not be accepted on the international market. In August, the U.K. stepped up the campaign by imposing a naval blockade against Iran.

In the process, they intercepted oil tankers off the Persian coast and prevented Iran from exporting petroleum to other countries. The British also prohibited the export of key commodities to Iran – such as sugar and steel – and froze Iranian bank accounts and assets in the U.K.
That same month, the U.K. evacuated its British technicians and closed Anglo-Iranian Oil Company refineries and other installations in the city of Abadan.

Mossadegh and his government assumed they could replace the technicians with those from other countries while training Iranians to fill the void. However, through legal threats and agreements, the British convinced other international oil companies in the United States and Europe, except Italy, to refrain from sending personnel.

Due to the British blockade and embargo, Iran’s petroleum production declined by about 96% and its oil income to almost zero between 1950 and 1952. At the same time, foreign oil companies like British Petroleum and Saudi Aramco doubled their production to offset the economic impact to the U.K. and the world of reduced or nonexistent production and exports from Iran.

Amid the economic crisis, Mossadegh’s inability to alleviate poverty, among other issues, caused his political coalition to fracture and fueled the British and American propaganda campaign against him ahead of his overthrow in Operation Ajax on Aug. 19, 1953.

A year later, the Shah of Iran, Mohammad Reza Pahlavi, consolidated power and signed an oil agreement with the British. In it, Iran’s share of the profits increased slightly, while an overwhelming majority of between 75% and 79% continued to be claimed by British and American companies. In exchange, the British lifted the blockade and enabled Iran to resume exporting oil on the international market.

The U.K.’s campaign to pressure Iran and oust its leader contains parallels with the current conflict. Now, just as then, a Western power is hoping to bring Iranian leadership to its knees – and encourage widespread anti-government protests – through coercive economic actions.
But contrary to the 1950s, Tehran today is better placed to deter its foreign adversary.

While Washington has drastically degraded Iran’s conventional military capabilities , including its air force and navy, Tehran has effectively employed drones, missiles and proxies to repeatedly strike U.S. assets in the region. Back in the 1950s, Iran had no network of sympathetic regional militias like it has today , and it lacked the sufficient technology to hit back at a conventionally superior military.

Iran can also counter economic measures. Since the war began in February 2026, Tehran and its partners have continuously targeted the tanker traffic and civilian and energy infrastructure of the Arab Gulf states.
Consequently, it has caused Gulf kingdoms to rethink remaining under the U.S. security umbrella and diversify defense partnerships to include other powers inside and outside the region.
Iran has also asserted control, to different degrees, over the critical choke points of the Strait of Hormuz and the Bab al-Mandab Strait in cooperation with the Houthis in Yemen.

By attacking the Arab Gulf states and disrupting commercial vessels in the region, Iran has driven up the price of oil and other commodities and exerted economic and political pressure on the United States and other countries.

And while the U.S. sanctions and other measures have exacerbated the formidable economic challenges facing Iran that predated the war – record currency devaluation , runaway inflation and contracted growth – the regime in Tehran has seemingly weathered the serious social unrest that transpired right before the conflict , during which thousands of protesters and other citizens took to the streets and were killed by the security forces.

Unlike Mossadegh, the current leaders of Iran have had decades to build up a resilience to outside pressure. And while it took two years of economic pressure to push Mossadegh from power, years of sanctions have to date failed to bring Iran’s Islamic Republic to its knees. There is no guarantee that increasing the pressure now will change that.
Eric Lob is affiliated with the Carnegie Endowment for International Peace.

articles.title: What Medicaid and ACA cuts mean for Washington
articles.author: Venice Buhain
paras: After last year's passage of HR1, the One Big Beautiful Bill put in place several changes that will decrease enrollment in Apple Health, Washington’s Medicaid program. Congress made changes to Medicaid to offset tax cuts in the 2025 bill.

One change is that adults aged 19 to 64 will have to work, train, or perform community service for at least 80 hours per month to keep their Apple Health coverage. Exceptions include being pregnant, being a primary caregiver, or having a medical condition. That requirement starts on Jan. 1. Furthermore, people in the program will have to prove their eligibility every six months, instead of every year.
Another change is that noncitizen adults like refugees and asylees who had been eligible for coverage will no longer be covered by Medicaid.
That means about 200,000 people in Washington state will lose their free or low-cost health coverage.

Ryan Moran, director of the Washington Health Care Authority, said that the state has taken measures to help people navigate the increased requirements, which will help about 400,000 of the 600,000 adults who would be affected stay on the program.
“But let us make no mistake, there will absolutely be coverage losses,” Moran said.

“The full effect of this will not be known until the end of 2027, and we at the state are trying to do everything that we can to preserve and mitigate coverage loss as these changes take effect,” he said.

And that’s not all. The changes also require states to reduce their supplemental funding to medical providers that are contracted to provide care to Medicaid patients. That is estimated to be a loss of $1.5 billion to Washington hospitals starting in 2028 -- which could mean higher costs for other patients either due to private insurance costs going up or hospitals having to rely more on charity care.
“That's more expensive for everyone, right?” Moran said.
Open enrollment for 2027 on the Washington Health Benefit Exchange is open and in the past few years, federal changes have made big impacts to health coverage accessibility in Washington state.

The first is the cuts to Medicaid, which provides health coverage for about 1.5 million adults and children in Washington state. Those cuts were included in what Trump called the One Big Beautiful Bill, which passed in 2025. Another is the continued impact of the loss of tax credits for people who purchase insurance through the Washington Health Benefit Exchange.
Recently, Sen. Patty Murray held a press conference to address these changes and how it will affect people as they sign up for health insurance in open enrollment.

“We've been knowing this coming. I've been talking to doctors and providers and health care clinics and hospitals all over our state about what that was going to mean to them. And now we are going to see the impact on people's health insurance when they pay for them,” Murray said.
The press conference was held a few days before the election.

At the press conference, Washington Insurance Commissioner Patty Kuderer added that on top of the loss of tax credits for marketplace health insurance, premiums are also rising, with an average increase of 22%.

“Nearly 280,000 people buy health coverage here if they don't get insurance through their employer, and most do so through our own state-based exchange,” Kuderer said. “And today, many people are feeling the sticker shock of the increased premiums.”
Murray said addressing health care costs would be one priority for Democrats in Congress.
“When we get back, we have to make sure that we work to reinstate the tax credits and fight to take these Medicaid cuts back,” she said.

articles.title: 'The Forge District': Kirkland Gives NE 85th Station Area a Rebrand
articles.author: Ryan Packer
paras: The City of Kirkland is hoping a new name for the area around a forthcoming bus rapid transit station can aid in revitalization efforts, after years of lackluster development activity there. Last week, the Kirkland City Council picked "The Forge District" as its preferred moniker for the area after considering several other alternatives for a rebrand that is intended to foster a "distinct identity" and punch up marketing for potential developers.

NE 85th Street Station, situated in the median of I-405, will see double-decker express bus service starting in 2029 as part of the Sound Transit S2 line , and existing ST Express buses will stop at the interchange as soon as next year. But the development spark that city leaders have been hoping to see in the immediate area has not yet caught fire, despite a 2023 rezone that provided significant development capacity.

About a mile from the heart of Kirkland's charming downtown, the 710-acre station area stands at the confluence of several other neighborhoods including Rose Hill, Everest, and Norkirk. Though the vision is a "thriving, new walkable district with high tech and family wage jobs, plentiful affordable housing, sustainable buildings, park amenities, and commercial and retail services linked by transit," the area remains dominated by car dealerships, drive-through businesses today, and the freeway looming overhead.

Following the selection of a name, a visual branding scheme will follow, "to create collateral to support retention and recruitment of businesses, property owners, developers, and investors," according to a staff report provided to councilmembers.

"When we talk about the naming for NE 85th, it's not just for us as current community members or business owners, but it is also looking at those who will be coming here in the future," Jen Davis Hayes, Kirkland's Economic Development Manager, said ahead of the final naming vote.

Why the Forge? "Heat, energy," noted a presentation created by the consultant company Watson Creative. "Complimentary juxtaposition to softer Rose Hill, Norkirk, Juanita, Houghton, Totem Lake, Bridle Trails."
"Scales well: Forge Building, Forge Station, Forge Park."

The Forge District also references the steel foundry built by the city's namesake, Peter Kirk, in 1890. That steel mill "never produced a single ingot," according to the Kirkland Heritage Society , and its closure in the wake of the 1893 national economic crisis prompted Kirk to retire away from the city that still bears his name.

"Early on this process, we had thought about ways to sort of honor Indigenous names, and for many very good reasons, we moved away from that," Deputy Mayor Neal Black said during a discussion in September. "And I think once we've moved away from that, this way of honoring the history, the steel mill, it's meaningful to me, and I think it could be meaningful to a lot of longtime Kirklanders."

The runners-up were The Rise District and The Union District, with a last-minute entrant provided by the Kirkland Heritage Society: the Kellett District. It was John George Kellett, another British businessman seeking his fortune in a sparsely-populated Eastside in the late 19th Century, that decided to name a fledgling town after Kirk. Among other reasons, that name was discarded as being potentially tricky for newcomers to spell.

Though Kirkland is clearly taking the idea of a marketing campaign as a way to raise the area's profile seriously, the future of the neighborhood will almost certainly hinge more on economics. Earlier this year, the Kirkland Council gave the 85th Station area zoning code another tweak intended to spur development, extending a "pioneer provision" that gives the first developers prepared to break ground a discount on affordable housing requirements through 2030.

Those tweaks also included added flexibility when it comes to future development agreements, potentially setting the stage for larger buildings than might otherwise be allowed under code today. Also included were prohibitions on townhome development throughout most of the area, a move intended to prevent the area from getting locked in to an underbuilt form.

The Council also took the step earlier this year of fully removing requirements for off-street parking within the entire station area, going further than a new state mandate in the hopes of providing maximum flexibility for potential builders.
But if the area is primed for a future boom, it hasn't arrived yet.

"We know that these areas are well-suited to accommodate future population and employment growth, and they also represent priority areas for transportation funding, so with that in mind we've recently done a lot of work to update the zoning in the station area to support the transportation investments," Kirkland Senior Planner LeAndra Baker-Lewis told the city's planning commission this past spring. "But we haven't seen a notable amount of development that would help bolster those investments."

Though the 85th station area isn't currently the most accommodating place to get around by walking or biking, Kirkland has been endeavoring to make inroads on that front as well. Just this fall, the City opened a new multiuse path connecting Downtown Kirkland and the future bus station. However, that project comes after Kirkland spent $3.7 million to add a third vehicle lane to NE 85th Street around 120th Avenue NE.

Though construction is well underway on Sound Transit's $2.4 billion Stride BRT program, which will include three total lines from Burien to Lynnwood, interest from developers when it comes to creating transit-oriented development near those future stations has been tepid at best.

In Renton, a recent rezone has primed the area around a Stride station that will include connections to two separate RapidRide lines, but builders are not yet beating down Renton's door to get their projects permitted there – a fact that stands in contrast with development activity around the 2 Line in Bellevue .
But there's a chance new Eastside residents would rather live in The Forge than in a neighborhood called Wilburton.

"Once one of these names is chosen, it would be interesting to talk about signage," Kirkland Councilmember John Tymczyszyn said last month. "Being called the Forge District would be a lot more interesting, in my opinion, if there was 100-foot-high steel sign when you drive up 85th and into this district, so that the name kind of resonates with people that visit that area."

articles.title: Ballard Starter Line
articles.author: Martin Pagel
paras: At the Ballard Town Hall meeting Sound Transit made it clear that they do not want to make any major changes to the BLE plans to avoid starting all over with the EIS process. They did consider at some point starting with a connection between Ballard and Westlake and delay or even skip the second downtown tunnel (DSTT2). But that would require a separate operations and maintenance facility (OMF) at Interbay or connecting to the existing downtown tunnel (DSTT1). The tunnel is old and surrounding soil is unstable and therefore they concluded this would be very risky and costly. Tom Terrific however suggested a single-track maintenance tunnel connection which would connect at the end of the current tunnel by the Convention Center.

While any major design change (such as an elevated line) may jeopardize the current EIS process, implementing a project in phases is common and accepted. Not spending $8b on a second downtown tunnel at this point would allow Sound Transit to connect Ballard much earlier (in particular if paired with other measures such as automating the line or a ship canal gondola ). With all the downtown complexities it would also reduce a lot of risks. And as almost half of the tunnel is covered by funds collected in Pierce and Snohomish County and the Eastside, it may even allow Sound Transit to finish the spine earlier, a goal the Board keeps reiterating.

Sound Transit has also stated that the Ballard line is necessary to connect to the Tacoma line as an Everett to Tacoma line would get too long for operators, but they could turn Tacoma trains around at Northgate or just change operators halfway.

Sound Transit studied alternatives for a second tunnel. Either the line could connect to the existing tunnel (interlining) by tapping into the existing tunnel at Pine St and 3rd or operate as a separate line with a separate OMF at Interbay. They determined that both options would not be any cheaper than proceeding with a second tunnel. I tend to agree with the risks involved with tapping the existing tunnel for interlining. However, Tom’s suggestion for a single track to connect a Ballard line with the existing tunnel should warrant further research. To reduce operational impact, such track could be used during off-hours. It would allow maintaining trains at the SODO OMF instead of having to build a separate OMF.

Before the original tunnel was extended to Capitol Hill with a slight curve to the south, it used to have a track extending straight east of the Westlake station for trains to turn around. It might be possible to extend that tunnel portion and add a north turn. You may need to use the I-5 Express Lane exit to build such track. That track could then connect with the Ballard line roughly at the Denny station. It would be fairly long but for a maintenance track that should not matter as much.

Adding such a maintenance tunnel would be expensive, but not nearly as much as building a second tunnel or a separate Interbay OMF. I hope it would allow Sound Transit to serve Ballard well before 2042.

articles.title: ‘Portuguese-style’ joins the fray as Port of Peri Peri Chicken prepares for the great Central Seattle chicken war of 2027
articles.author: CHS Staff
paras: (Image: Port of Peri Peri Chicken Kirkland)
The walk down 12th Ave can open up access to a wealth of food and drink alternatives beyond the Capitol Hill core.
A few like L’Oursin at 14th and Jefferson have stood the test of time .
Two new projects are taking shape in a recent mixed use building on a block of 12th Ave that saw a skirmish over small business displacement play out during the project’s development.
Paperwork shows the new restaurants taking shape together on the street level of the Tapestry apartments building at 12th and Fir.
One space is being prepared for Cheng’s Dumplings and Noodle , a Taiwanese concept from first-time Seattle restaurateurs Ya-Tzu Cheng and Yu-Fen Liu.

The other will be home to an expansion of Port of Peri Peri Chicken , a fast-casual restaurant chain specializing in Portuguese-style flame-grilled chicken seasoned with African bird’s eye chilis. The franchise chain already has locations in Kirkland and Bothell among nearly 30 outlets in 11 states nationwide.
The arrival of Port of Peri Peri will add to what has become a comically intense wave of new chicken openings across the Capitol Hill area.

High profile investments include the arrival of the San Francisco-born Starbird Chicken chain on E Pike in a portion of the block’s emptied Amazon grocery store and Char the Chicken , the launch of a new grilled poultry concep t from the backers of the scuttled Mt. Joy chicken sandwich chain and a popular food influencer.

Meanwhile, the recent food and drink history on 12th Ave where Cheng’s and the new Port of Peri Peri are being planned includes the unsuccessful fight for Saba Ethiopian to keep its space after it lost its lease on the block amid plans for demolition to make way for the development six years ago.

articles.title: Seattle Center Diwali celebration pushes through disruption by far-right influencers
articles.author: Justin Carder
paras: Community members and families celebrating Diwali at the Seattle Center Armory on Saturday pushed through an attempt by activists to disrupt the festivities.

The confrontation occurred during youth cultural performances at the annual Diwali: Lights of India festival. Attendees stepped in to eject the disruptors — a couple far-right political activists and internet personalities who frequently stage confrontations at public demonstrations and cultural gatherings and some hangers-on — before the situation could escalate further, ensuring the free, all-day celebration continued as scheduled.

King County Executive Girmay Zahilay condemned the hostility and commended the resilience of the gathering. “Diwali celebrates the triumph of light over darkness,” Zahilay said in a statement. “Those who came to spread fear will not define this holiday, and they will not define King County.”
In the wake of the confrontation, Seattle Center and festival organizers underscored ongoing security and safety coordination across the Festál cultural series.

Saturday’s disruption came amid escalated concern and tightened security at Seattle Center, elements the group behind the disruption were surely aware of. The campus was the scene of a deadly shootout this summer during the Bite of Seattle event.
There were no announced arrests in Saturday’s incident.

The Coalition of Hindus of North America called on authorities to confront bias targeting the community. In its statement, CoHNA stressed protecting cultural gatherings. “Unfortunately the response from authorities has been slow or lacking, with a reluctance to even name or call out the anti-Hindu bigotry driving many of these actions,” the organization said.
Presented by nonprofit Northwest SHARE as part of the Seattle Center Festál series, the festival filled the hall with classical dance and music.

Seattle Mayor Katie Wilson , who attended another celebration with her child, denounced the stunt and effort to cause chaos at the festival. “We condemn the hateful nonsense from bigots who interrupted a beautiful Diwali ceremony at Seattle Center,” the mayor said in a statement.

articles.title: Surfeit Rock
articles.author: Dave Segal
paras: The inaugural Baba Obscura festival took over a hot zone in Pioneer Square November 5–8, and if you had the energy and alertness, you could’ve crammed a month’s worth of compelling music into four nights. With Freakout Fest on hiatus, Baba Obscura had big shoes to fill, and it did so admirably. There were some minor hitches and late start times, and the sets at Baba Yaga seemed to draw far larger crowds than those at AXIS and Central Saloon, but overall things seemed to run smoothly. Here are some highlights that I experienced. Your mileage will surely vary.

FROND Seattle quartet Frond were in progress when I entered Baba Yaga, and their Cocteau Twins-lite shoegaze songs were spectral and woozy, with vocalist Jewel Loree—who also plays in the Grizzled Mighty and Golden Idols and hosts KEXP’s Astral Plane show—finessing some nice dubby bass lines. Then a switch seemingly flicked and they launched into high-energy psych-rock, followed by a Wooden Shjips-style motorik jam. What a pleasant surprise. Frond currently have no music online, but you should keep tabs on them.

WEEP WAVE Seattle trio Weep Wave present as blue-collar hard-rockers, but, thankfully, they are so much more than that. Sure, they have their share of melodic anthems that would please fans of Protomartyr or the Hold Steady. But beyond the meaty and torqued guitar and bass riffing in their existential songs about space and death, there be weird electronic elements and club-friendly beats that emanate from a synth off to the side of the stage. Boozy, air-punching rock can merge with EDM (plus some sine waves reminiscent of Kraftwerk ca. Radio-Activity ) and get the ladies—and fellas—moving. And I heard some deceptive funkiness à la Led Zeppelin and Blurt in a couple of songs, while another possessed the fierce vibes of Killing Joke’s “Wardance.” Interesting rock is not a plentiful commodity in 2026, but Weep Wave deliver a potent metallic KO onstage. Look out for them.

JJUUJJUU Led by Desert Daze boss Phil Pirrone , JJUUJJUU unabashedly reveled in free-flowing psychedelia from the get-go. The pick-up band included cowboy-hatted Night Beats guitarist Danny “Lee Blackwell” Rajan, who served as the wild card, generating wild guitar eruptions amid the three long improvisations. Combining grandiloquent stoner-rock with instrumental sprawl à la the Doors’ “The End” and Perrone’s occasional old-school, longhair-rock howl, JJUUJJUU revived the spirit of the on-hiatus Freakout Fest. They also had a very cool motorik cruiser, which would become the motif among the groups I saw at BO.

SPOON BENDERS Portland trio Spoon Benders’ churning frenzy of garage-rock, psych-rock, and punk triggered a mosh pit that became increasingly large and violent throughout their Baba Yaga set. It felt like the floor was buckling—maybe because one of the moshers was a mountainous dude who could’ve been a Seahawks offensive tackle. Bassist Kate Black sang with the angsty gravitas of Thalia Zedek and Jennifer Herrema while drummer Mike Amster flexed rapid-fire fills à la Keith Moon. Guitarist Leo Pastor kept things swerving and bruising—just like the human bumper cars in the pit.

MDOU MOCTAR What a whiplash transition this was. Sans band, Nigerian guitarist Mdou Moctar sat down with his electric guitars and unspooled raw desert-blues virtuosity, peppering that with soulful plaints in his native Tamasheq and shouts of “Go!” The loving crowd clapped along nearly continuously to his sinuous riffs that could’ve spiraled on to infinity with no complaints. He also told a long, charming anecdote about how one can learn more from travel than from reading books. ‘Twas a privilege to witness.

PACKAGING Arriving a bit late to Packaging’s AXIS performance, I encountered them in sluggish ballad/slack shoegaze mode. Eventually, though, they bestowed a krautrock banger upon us that displayed them at their aerodynamic best. Damn near everyone’s gotta have a motorik jam these days, which is as it should be. For the last song, Packaging broke out the Vibra-Tone and flute, which more rock groups ought to be doing. This abstract intro led into a ferocious krautrock steamroller that aspired to the zenith of Can’s “Mother Sky.” You gotta aim high, y’all.

ROSE CITY BAND Dag, after packing out Tractor Tavern last December, Portland’s Rose City Band played to maybe 40 patrons at AXIS. A travesty for a Friday midnight slot, but that didn’t deter guitarist/singer Ripley Johnson’s bearded, nonchalantly brilliant bros from turning this mother out with an economy of movement that would’ve impressed J.J. Cale . Easygoing, cosmic country rock is RCB’s default setting, and they are the greatest modern practitioners of that art. All of the musicians are masterly, but Barry Walker Jr. on pedal steel really launches RCB to the most exalted plane of the genre. And as their set wore on, I became convinced that Johnson’s guitar tone resides on the godly level of the aforementioned Cale’s, Jerry Garcia’s, and Agitation Free’s Lutz “Lüül” Graf-Ulbrich’s. Did RCB have a motorik joint, too? Of course , silly, and it ruled. At one point, though, RCB shockingly detoured into a shimmering disco/yacht-rock number, replete with the beat from Hall & Oates’ “I Can’t Go for That (No Can Do).” Reader, it worked! Wish you were there.

NATHAN NOTHING Nathan Nothing (aka Nate Quiroga) ain’t your typical synth-wielding electronic musician. No static, furrowed-brow stage demeanor for him. The former Mad Rad MC/producer and Iska Dhaaf leader instead jumps around, dances, and bounds into the crowd to rap and sing in an FX’d chipmunk voice about poverty, punching Nazis, and feeding the poor and eating the rich. With ex-Crypts member Bryce Brown on drums and Night Fortress’s Blair Field on downtuned guitar, Nathan Nothing creates clubby goth music that leaves disco balls in shards. There’s dilapidated house music, brutish, song-based electronic music in the Meat Beat Manifesto vein, and even the odd post-punkish ballad. But mostly, these are dance-in-the-ashes dystopia soundtracks. For makers of such dark music, they emit good, positive energy.

THE SPYRALS I only caught about 15 minutes of LA trio the Spyrals’ set, but their stripped-down, ’60s-rooted garage-psych displayed crafty songwriting and excellent dynamics. A pity I had to exit early to see the Gories, who went on 13 minutes after their designated start time.

THE GORIES “I forgot to tune my guitar, so you’re in for it,” announced Mick Collins before the legendary Detroit garage-rock group’s incendiary performance in Baba Yaga’s absolutely packed basement. (Yes, Collins has moved to Brooklyn, but he’ll always be a Detroiter to the core.) No matter, as Collins and Dan Kroha’s dual, barbed-wire guitar attack cut through bullshit rock excesses with their usual primitive cunning. Along with drummer Peggy O’Neill, the Gories pare rock, soul, and blues (the latter two repped by ace covers of Eddie Holland’s “Leavin’ Here” and John Lee Hooker’s “Boogie Chillen”) to their most vital essences. O’Neill’s kit includes snare, tom, tambourine, and no cymbals. She makes Mo Tucker sound like Neil Peart. It’s not easy to do this without sounding like bloodless museum curators, but the Gories are ultimate real ones in the underground, and have been for four decades. They still got it, and then some.

THE INTELLIGENCE Former Stranger Music Genius Lars Finberg left Seattle for California many years ago, and a lot has changed with his music since then. I’d somehow missed his last few albums, in which he ditches his wry garage-rock subversions for a bizarre electronic-music direction, but with interludes of odd-cadenced crooning and guitarlele (?!) strumming. “What are you laughing at, man? It’s the only guitar I can afford,” Finberg quipped to scattered chuckles. Bedecked in an oversized ballcap and green Converse All Stars at a sparsely attended Central Saloon, Finberg sat behind a Crumar Mojo keyboard and began with some spacey jazz-fusion that explains why he titled his latest album Witches Woo . His was a set of baffling tangents, which one hardly ever sees/hears anymore. A downer, Nilsson-ian ballad segued into a killer bleepy techno cut. A Señor Coconut-esque cha-cha preceded a funky, µ-Ziq-like chiller. During one excellent banger, Finberg shouted, “That sounds like Ten Inch Nails [ sic ]. Give it up for Chris the sound guy!” The Intelligence’s crowd may have been unjustly minuscule, but everyone there went home with a unique memory. Do you know how rare that is?

ZOOKRAUGHT My first Zookraught show—a benefit for orgs helping Palestinians—happened last year under a bridge in an unlovable part of SODO. The DIY/off-the-grid nature of that gig seemed like the Seattle threesome’s ideal habitat. So it was a bit strange to witness them in a conventional club, but they thrived there, too. Zookraught make careening post-punk with serious fuck-or-fight energy. They sweat revolutionary queer youth power. Primal-scream catharsis is their default mode, and they’re artful with it, despite (because?) of all the chaos sparking around them. Zookraught draw you in with their colorful, unusual appearance and keep you riveted—and riotously moshing—with exceptional command of their instruments. They seem destined for much bigger things.

THE BLACK TONES Talented twins Eva and Cedric Walker have added a guitarist, bassist, and keyboardist to the Black Tones, the better to manifest their more expansive new album, Diamond Ruby Night , their first in seven years. Speaking of additions, did Cedric gain more muscle? His drumming sure seemed to indicate so. Anyway, Central Saloon felt way too small for the Black Tones’ arena-ready goth-leaning rock and new wave. The Diamond Ruby Night songs’ subjects are dark (mental health issues, encounters with prison inmates whom Eva’s met, death, etc.), but the music’s uplifting. Right now, I like the early Black Tones incarnation a little better, but the new version is very accomplished and leaves me wondering if opening slots on upcoming tours by U2, the Cure, or Echo & the Bunnymen are out of the question.

THE BLACK ANGELS The music airing over the PA before Austin, Texas psych-rockers the Black Angels took the stage at a clusterfucked Showbox was fantastic, and likely chosen by the band. Songs by Bruce Haack, Pearls Before Swine, the United States of America, Wolfgang Dauner, and the Zombies, among others, proved that they have impeccable taste. I wish that the Black Angels’ music were as interesting as their record collection.

Don’t get me wrong—the Black Angels are fine, and they still have the ability to draw 1,130 punters on a Sunday night. But I’ve never understood the fuss that many have made over them. Despite the majesty of many of their songs, the Black Angels strike me as Psych 101—basic and straitlaced. A slow and sinister tune such as “Black Grease” is cool, but its similarity to Loop’s “Too Real to Feel” reveals how that British group imbue the blueprint with more edge and lysergic potency.

Anyway, the Black Angels are currently celebrating the 20th anniversary of their debut album, Passover , which they pretty faithfully replicated. It’s a remarkably consistent album, verging on the monolithic. The dominant style is menacing, methodical, and rhythmically blocky, with rudimentary rock riffs blown out to massive dimensions through FX and punishing volume; my ears are still ringing, even though I wore quality earplugs. Whoever was working sound had everything dialed in wonderfully, especially Misti Hamrick and Jake Garcia’s basses.

A friend at the show summed up the Black Angels’ tempos with a gesture: moving his hand horizontally across his torso in a straight line. It took till the 11th track, “Bad Vibrations,” for a rave-up to appear. “Push It” featured the only real danceable beats. “Firefly” introduced a rare diversion with a more buoyant and whimsical tone. And I dug the liturgical Spiritualized vibe of the intro to “Call to Arms.”

Folks began to file out of the club in droves around 10:45 p.m. (90 minutes into the set), but if you stayed till the end, you were rewarded with the night’s most exciting cut, the outré freakout—à la Mercury Rev’s “Syringe Mouth,” albeit not as wild—known as “Molly Moves My Generation.”

It’s weird to be the lone dispassionate observer in a sea of devotees; my ears are still ringing from their cheers. But I’m happy for everyone who loves the Black Angels, and the band did brisk business at the merch table.

articles.title: Stranger Suggests: Your Agenda This Week, November 9–15
articles.author: Julianne Bell
paras: (MUSIC) For over 40 years in Pussy Galore, Blues Explosion, Boss Hog, and other feral units, ex-Ivy Leaguer Jon Spencer has adopted a lewd, shit-kicking persona, the better to make rock and roll sound savage, gritty, and reckless. It’s a shtick, sure, but Spencer’s utterly riveting with it. Even in his 60s, dude still rages. Late-career garage-rock heaters such as Spencer Sings the Hits! , Sick of Being Sick! , and the new Songs of Personal Loss and Protest prove that Jon can still find countless ways to transform primal urges into sonic art. With drummer Spider Bowman and bassist Kendall Wind in tow, Spencer continues to convert his anger at the state of the world and sadness over personal hardships into adrenaline-spiking, soul-inflating rock. ( Sunset Tavern, 8 pm, 21+ ) DAVE SEGAL
Ms. Lauryn Hill & Wyclef Jean: Celebrating 30 years of Fugees’ The Score

(MUSIC) Lauryn Hill is one of hip-hop’s truly outstanding rappers. Her name is on two albums in the hip-hop canon—the Fugees’ The Score (1996) and her solo work The Miseducation of Lauryn Hill (1998). There is also the raw boom-bap/dancehall style track “Lost Ones,” which is on Miseducation . It alone put any doubt about her skills on the mic in the grave and solidified her reputation among the elite. And this, ultimately, is what matters in the game or rap and reality: her mic skills, her impeccable record, her undying commitment to what has almost entirely vanished from present-day rhymes; namely, “saying something” and never “fakin’ the funk.” So, let’s just show Hill the respect she deserves; few golden era rappers can match her accomplishments. ( Climate Pledge Arena, 8 pm, all ages ) CHARLES MUDEDE

(MUSIC) When the world is on fire, radical compassion is one weapon, and trauma-bonding through bleak, back-alley art-rap is another. There are only two options. Armand Hammer, the binary star comprising New York rappers billy woods and Elucid, has that medicine, and their latest effort, last year’s acclaimed Mercy , a second team-up with everywhere man The Alchemist, takes the world to task. Politics, social ills, and petty annoyances are all handled with typical street corner soothsayer panache, woods stringing together rap-noir micro vignettes that Elucid bounces right back in the form of raspy, big picture, stream-of-consciousness bars. Never ones for undue optimism, the two emcees have nevertheless hit middle age with a head full of steam, itself a testament to the ability to thrive in the face of the static we’re all forced to wade through daily. AH continues to be a crucial antidote for the common ill, and only seems to be getting better with time. ( Crocodile, 8 pm, all ages ) TODD HAMM

(LITERATURE) Andrew Joseph White’s 2022 dystopian fantasy horror young adult novel Hell Followed With Us established him as an author to watch and attracted the notice of The Matrix director Lilly Wachowski, who is currently co-producing an anime-inspired film adaptation. His first book for adults, 2025’s You Weren’t Meant to Be Human , is a gruesome, transgressive trans body horror tale set in Appalachia. White incorporates his experience as a trans bi man with autism into his books and uses fear to plumb the terrors of our present-day existence. His newest book, You’re No Better , is a young adult psychological thriller about Morgan, a 17-year-old autistic trans boy who testified against his own serial killer father, putting him behind bars. He must prove to a predatory true crime documentary crew and his own mother that he is nothing like his dad. Given the relentless demonization of trans teens in the news lately, this novel’s message couldn’t be more timely or urgent. ( Third Place Books Lake Forest Park, 7 pm ) JULIANNE BELL

(FOOD) Show up to Ravenna Brewing on Thursday to slurp four soups whipped up by four local breweries and restaurants all vying to be the winner of the coveted Golden Ladle. It is Ravenna’s fifth annual Battle of the Soups. This year the competition includes Hopvine Pub, Watershed Pub, Layers, and Big Time Brewery. All benefits go to Washington Wild. All soup goes into your belly. What soups will they be? It’s a secret. Tickets cost $25 and get you a 5 ounce serving of each soup. ( Ravenna Brewing, 5–7 pm ) NATHALIE GRAHAM

(PERFORMANCE) Alex Tatarsky, who once made headlines by pulling a hoax at the Andy Kaufman Awards in 2013, where they announced they were Andy’s daughter and that he was still alive, says their absurdist performances live in “the uncomfortable in-between zone of comedy, dance-theater, performance art, and deluded rant—sometimes with songs.” Their solo show Sad Boys in Harpy Land was commissioned by and premiered at Abrons Arts Center in 2023 before transferring Off-Broadway to Playwrights Horizons later that year and comes to On the Boards November 12–14. In their “magnum o-pussy,” Tatarsky reanimates tortured characters from sources ranging from Seinfeld to Goethe and collages them into a bildungsroman about “a young Jewish woman who thinks she is a small German boy who thinks he is a tree.” Experimental electronic musician Shane Riley, director Iris McCloughan, set designer Andreea Mincic, and lighting designer Masha Tsimring also contribute to the “tour de farce.” It’s not for the faint of heart—be prepared for chewed-up sardines and mandatory audience participation—but you may walk away feeling a little less alone in our current dystopian nightmare. Read the full interview with Alex from our November issue . ( On the Boards, 7:30 pm ) JULIANNE BELL
Radio Gaza & Wo’Pop Present: A Benefit For Palestine

(MUSIC/FUNDRAISER) If you’ve been feeling helpless on your doomscroll, here is something positive for you to actually do! Radio Gaza is a series that uplifts and celebrates Palestinian culture through music, art, poetry, and fundraising. Their next event is at Clock-Out Lounge and will benefit the organization Heal Palestine. The night is co-presented by KEXP’s Wo’Pop, and the lineup includes musicians Clarissa Bitar, Shelby Natasha, Intisaar (who was just featured on The Stranger ’s live music podcast, Noise Complaint ), PEN, and KEXP DJ Jyoti B.Fly. There will also be henna tattoos by Jo Sleem, poetry and Tatreez art by Hala Saleh, merch by Sweetmalson, and art from Seattle Artists for Palestine. All of this, plus Arabic treats and beverages by Ya Hala. ( Clock-Out Lounge, 8 pm, 21+ ) NICO SWENSON

(LITERATURE) New York-based author Min Jin Lee is best known for her sprawling Korean family epic masterpiece Pachinko , which was a 2017 finalist for the National Book Award for Fiction and spawned a similarly critically acclaimed TV adaptation on Apple TV+ in 2022. Almost a decade after Pachinko , she’s back with her highly anticipated follow-up American Hagwon , which is just as ambitious in its scope. The novel follows the saga of the Koh family, which includes parents John and Helen and their three children—Bo, DH, and Mido. After their peaceful middle-class life in Korea is torn apart, they must leave Seoul for Sydney and then Southern California, where they grapple with a new reality, start over from scratch, and grasp for a better future. “Hagwon” refers to a Korean tutoring center, where students strive for excellence, and the book asks questions about the faith we place in academic institutions and the cost of pursuing success. Like Pachinko , it’s a nuanced critique of the American Dream and a portrait of the Korean diaspora, and the Kohs will root themselves in your memory forever over the 656 pages. ( Meany Hall, 7:30 pm ) JULIANNE BELL

(VISUAL ART) About an hour’s drive north of Seattle, there’s a magical place called Pilchuck Glass School where the world’s top glass artists convene throughout the year to whip miraculous glass art into existence in boiling hot shops and less-hot cold shops. The campus is a work of art in its own right: It spreads out like a 1970s hobbit fantasy complete with forests threaded with secret paths, stained-glass follies, and treehouses where acolytes retire to revel at the end of a long day’s work. The school isn’t typically accessible to the public, which makes the annual Light the Forest even more special. The event—a self-guided walking tour—unfolds on two dusky November nights, during which the already-ensorcelling Pilchuck campus transforms into an immersive light installation ablaze with neon. This year’s artists are Seattle-based glass baddies MiNHi England and John Sharvin (who both appeared on season 3 of Blown Away ). Did I mention it’s magical? I can’t overemphasize how utterly enchanted it is. This year, they’re also offering day-of workshops, so you can walk away with your very own neon creation or hand-blown ornaments. ( Pilchuck Glass School ) AMANDA MANITACH
