articles.title: Op-Ed: 'Building Charm' Book Offers Guide to Developing Outstanding Neighborhoods
articles.author: Naama Blonder
paras: The following is an excerpt from Chapter 1 of Building Charm: A Hyper-Practical Guide to Developing Outstanding New Neighborhoods by Naama Blonder and Misha Bereznyak, founders of Smart Density. Drawing on international experience and years of hands-on work, Building Charm presents a proven, practical system for creating genuinely appealing neighborhoods, one developed within real-world development and municipal constraints and applicable across a wide range of densities, from low-rise settings to complex high-density environments. Learn more at smartdensity.com .
Why do even our most thoughtful new neighborhoods lack the charm found in older places?

The departure of Modernist planning from traditional patterns of city building, and the problems it created, have been widely discussed and are now well understood. And while these Modernist planning ideas still dominate in many places, it is generally accepted that we now have a superior set of ideas and practices, and they can deliver neighborhoods of the same quality as our older neighborhoods.

These ideas and practices generally follow what we call the prevailing urbanist model — a widely shared contemporary framework for urban development that prioritizes reduced reliance on cars, walkability and cycling infrastructure, access to public transit, well-defined streets and parks, and often medium to high densities with mixed uses. This model represents what is widely considered best practice among urban planners and designers, and it has shaped many of the more successful new neighborhoods built in recent decades.

But while some new neighborhoods can teach a lot about innovative ideas and the implementation of best practices, when it comes to matching the experience that many old neighborhoods provide so successfully, they have surprisingly little to offer.

It took us time to recognize that the prevailing urbanist model itself had fundamental limitations. Both of us had grown up and practiced in places still shaped by Modernist planning, where any improvement felt significant. At that time, relatively few neighborhoods had been built according to the principles of the prevailing urbanist model, making it easy to attribute any shortcomings to implementation issues or local conditions rather than to flaws in the model itself.

However, the shortcomings of the neighborhoods and the principles that produced them became apparent over time: at first, as the novelty of such neighborhoods wore off, and even more so later, after our own attempts to implement the principles of the prevailing urbanist model met with little success in achieving the qualities of traditional cities.
We had a few opportunities to work on projects that appeared to have great potential, but with the design tools we were using, those projects yielded only mundane results.

In a project in the Greater Toronto Area, we were retained to create a vision to transform a 100-hectare area of low-intensity commercial and logistic uses near a train station into a dense, mixed-use community. We worked within a new street network that had already been planned, but we otherwise had a significant level of freedom in the design. We applied the leading principles of the prevailing urbanist model, and also identified a unique opportunity to create a continuous secondary network of mid-block connections that enriched the experience and the opportunities in the neighborhood. However, even at the level of a vision plan, it became clear that the constraints imposed by the pre-established street network would not allow us to achieve our aim.

Another project, in Southeast Asia, initially appeared promising. This project had a spectacular setting, with an existing network of irrigation and flood control canals. Other development projects in the area ignored the opportunity they presented, and usually filled most of the canals. We decided early to take a different approach and integrate the canals in the design, which created an attractive quality. Despite this strong start, as the design developed, it became increasingly clear that its overall character would end up typical of new development in the area, especially in the street experience, which is a critical factor in shaping the feel of a neighborhood. This was disappointing — not because the design wasn’t unique, but because, even with the integration of the canals, we still couldn’t achieve the character and qualities found in older neighborhoods with canals or even in more ordinary older neighborhoods in the same region. While in the previous project we’d been limited by a pre-existing framework, here we were limited mainly by our own ideas.

The failures that we experienced directly and, more importantly, the disappointment we felt when visiting neighborhoods designed by the brightest designers in the field convinced us that we were all still doing something wrong.

articles.title: Seattle Times Columnist Still Struggling with Middle Housing Concept
articles.author: Doug Trumm
paras: Seattle Times opinion columnist Alex Fryer is back at it with some deep housing thoughts. His Sunday column titled " How to fix Seattle’s ‘middle housing’ mess " piece is a mess in its own right.

Whether through willful ignorance or sincere befuddlement, Fryer is pretty lost when it comes to middle housing. He gets the basic timeline correct: state lawmakers passed a middle housing law in 2023 setting a minimum standard that that had to be in place by July 2025 for major cities like Seattle.

Seattle used an interim ordinance to enact middle housing zoning changes to beat the clock after the Harrell administration struggled mightily to put together a Comprehensive Plan and keep it on schedule. The last-minute route Harrell chose means zoning changes have been in place just over a year, and Fryer is ready to begin drawing sweeping conclusions with one year of data.

"The early results of HB 1110 are in, and they are not good — for affordability, the environment or Seattle’s once-vaunted quality of life," Fryer writes. "Construction permits filed with the city since an interim middle housing ordinance went into effect in July 2025 show that four freestanding houses on a single lot is the predominant type of what Seattle City Hall calls middle housing."

The one-year snapshot of data presented by the Seattle Times shows 65 projects that add four freestanding homes on one lot, 52 projects that add a pair of duplexes, and 30 projects that add a duplex plus two freestanding homes. That's 588 homes in all, on 147 lots that typically only would have had a single home.

While some of those lots might have added a backyard cottage or basement apartment under previous zoning, the fourplex reform appears to have been an incentive for more projects to break ground, and add more housing in doing so.

So far, fourplexes are a small piece of Seattle's overall housing production – which delivers around 10,000 new homes in an average year – and that's not likely to change drastically. That said, it's an important housing option for a certain contingent of people in need of family-sized housing, trying to leave the rental market, or looking to downsize from larger homes.

Enacting fourplex zoning and seeing an uptick in fourplex construction is basically what the law was designed to do. Fryer has fixated on the idea that the fourplexes should be attached rather than freestanding, which he never fully explains.

"Older homes purchased and then razed. Entire lots bulldozed and scraped of every living thing," Fryer writes, melodramatically. "Although the language of HB 1110 promised buildings that are 'compatible in scale, form, and character with single-family houses …,' the result so far has been architectural gigantism: Tall, bulky homes that take up every allowable inch of land and often sell for more than a million dollars."

Reading between the lines, Fryer's argument seems to be that attached housing would be cheaper, less carbon-intensive, and create more space for trees and greenery. However, a fourplex taking the place of a oneplex or duplex is going to increase housing access and moderate prices regardless of whether the walls touch or not. Anyone who has browsed housing listings recently can see why: similar townhomes command similar prices whether their walls touch or not.

Another key fact Fryer overlooks: a townhome is almost always cheaper than a single family home in the same neighborhood. Fryer's is an argument by lazy anecdote; he does not cite anything approaching a comprehensive analysis of new house prices. In fact, the only specific project he cited was the same South Park townhome project he wrote about last year, which despite all Fryer's snobbish fretting about aesthetics and tree canopy, sold for less than $500,000 each, as The Urbanist pointed out in a rebuttal .

The phenomenon of single family tear downs was longstanding and not invented with the middle housing law. The difference is now some teardowns result in fourplexes rather than almost exclusively larger single family homes. The status quo before the law was not good for affordability.

The previous status quo came with no guarantees around tree canopy either. In fact, single family zones lost tree canopy even in periods when fourplexes were banned, accounting for 87 acres of net canopy loss from 2016 to 2021, according to the City's official tree assessment. Far denser multifamily and mixed-use zones accounted for almost all of Seattle's considerable housing growth over that period while essentially treading water on canopy, losing just 24 acres on net, as more than 40,000 new homes went in.

The holy grail for urbanists and others focused on housing affordability was never simply to unlock fourplex townhomes alone. Many had an eye toward denser housing forms, like stacked flats, in formerly single family zones. Fryer briefly brings up that the middle housing reform also allowed for sixplexes within a quarter mile of frequent transit or if two homes are built as affordable housing. That undersells the multiplex possibility .

Thanks to density bonuses for tree preservation and/or adding affordable homes, 12-unit stacked flat complexes are a possibility on some lots. That segment from sixplexes to 12-plexes are likely to be even more affordable than fourplexes and open up formerly single family neighborhoods to renters in a far bigger way.
Architects like Matt Hutchins publicized this burgeoning opportunity, but even Hutchins admitted stacked flats would be a bit of unicorn, with townhomes the workhorse bulk product.

“We’re talking about like maybe 5% of the townhouse projects become stacked flat projects,” Hutchins told The Urbanist in 2025. “There’s still significant headwinds that are going to drive people into the safe harbor of four townhouses. However, there are now avenues, I think, for more ambitious developers who want to take advantage of these [stacked flat] incentives that, really have the right site, and have the right mission.”

But rather than focus on reforms to make tree-preserving stacked flats more of the norm, Fryer bought into a far-fetched preservation-focused idea from the slow growth crowd. The latest get-off-my-lawn coalition has branded themselves Seattle Residents for Thoughtful Growth, and their idea is divide up existing large single family homes to create more housing, rather than focusing on new construction.

"Here’s their concept: Take an existing house and split up each floor. Add a kitchen and bath in the rear on each level, and you have two, three or four new units," Fryer wrote. "Construction is fast, they say, because the existing foundation and structure remains."

That "concept" is a red herring – almost never practical and rarely feasible for the vast majority of properties. Fryer grants that reforms to development standards would be needed, suggesting the City "mandate smaller spaces, which would be cheaper for homebuyers." He doesn't explain how that would work, exactly. Hutchins called it a "wishfully naive idea" – adding turning houses into triplexes "is legal today, but not economically viable, otherwise it would be happening."

Dividing existing homes is expensive and complicated. It entails moving walls and adding bathrooms, kitchens, laundry spaces, and new secured entries and stairs – all of which is pricey. No one from Fryer's camp has demonstrated this will result in affordable housing, especially when factoring in the high cost of procuring a single family home. To make home subdivision practical, an especially large house is needed, which is usually priced accordingly.

Fryer's blind spot around housing seems to tied to his own experience as a Seattle homeowner. Fryer and his spouse own a nearly 2,400-square-foot home valued at more than $1.1 million per RedFin. The Fryers bought this 1946-built Admiral District home in 2005 for $438,000 according to King County property records. Now, 21 years later the house has nearly tripled in value, making them the owners of a million-dollar asset thanks to the dysfunctions of the Seattle housing market.

Unlike a renter, Fryer has a financial incentive for Seattle's housing market to stay overheated, and he lacks the same visceral urgency to solve the problem. His mortgage payment is still locked in at 2005 bargain prices regardless of what direction the housing market takes.

While Fryer was able to get in while Seattle home prices were still fairly attainable for the median-income earner, that's not the reality for first-time homebuyers today. The gain for homeowners like Fryer has been everyone else's pain. And to add salt in the wound, they claim new housing is the problem and cry crocodile tears for million-dollar house prices when that's exactly what is propping up their personal fortunes.

Fryer is happy to mandate smaller homes carved out of aging housing stock for new buyers while living in a spacious 2,400-square-foot home himself. He didn't say if he would volunteer his own home for this cellular division treatment.
The famous proverb applies to housing policy: People who live in glass houses shouldn't throw stones, especially when that house is worth more than one million dollars.

Fryer is not just some guy. In addition to having a regular column in the region's largest paper, he sits on the Seattle Times editorial board, which issues one of the most influential set of endorsements in the Puget Sound region and often backs more conservative candidates and causes. They typically oppose new tax measures, even when they fund transit or housing investments that lower cost of living for working class Seattleites. For example, the editorial board opposed the successful 2025 ballot measure funding social housing via a high earners tax.

Earlier this year, the board dubbed The Urbanist a " builder's mouthpiece " while complaining about the composition of an internal meeting at city hall to discuss how to advance bolder zoning changes .

Simply put, Fryer is out of touch, and it shows. While Fryer and friends are keeping close tabs on tree removal permits and each "bigleaf maple" that bites the dust, the number of renters and first-time homebuyers being priced out of Seattle does not seem to faze them or grab their interest in quite the same way.

Millennials and Zoomers are in a tough position when it comes to housing, and the policy changes and cultural norms Fryer is pushing would add fuel to the fire. Seattleites deserve a real variety and abundance of housing options in every neighborhood, not vague promises of divvying up old homes because we are too scared and architecturally picky to build anything new.

On one issue Fryer is right. Housing affordability is likely to be a huge issue in next year's election: "Next fall, seven Seattle City Council positions are up for grabs. Middle housing — real middle housing — ought to be part of the campaign."
Voters, however, are likely to see through flimsy ideas that have no real shot at moving the needle on affordability.

articles.title: Council Debates Seattle's Future Budget Sustainability
articles.author: Amy Sundberg
paras: This week Seattle Budget Chair Dan Strauss presented his budget balancing package amending Mayor Katie Wilson’s proposed 2027-2028 budget . In spite of a less than stellar revenue forecast in October, Strauss was able to find plenty of money to allow councilmembers to include their own priorities into the budget proposal, although some councilmembers ended up a little better off than others.
All together, the balancing package adds more than $50 million in council priorities for 2027 alone.

“This proposal makes critical investments that will deliver real results: reversing cuts to firefighters, making historic investments in housing and homelessness, and clearing violent crime case backlogs. It does it all while erasing deficits and balancing the city’s budget through 2030,” Strauss said.

Strauss opted to transfer the entire amount of extra Jumpstart payroll tax revenue predicted in the most recent forecast, as well as an off-cycle Jumpstart payment, into the General Fund to fund councilmember priorities to the tune of $23 million. The Jumpstart tax was originally intended to go mostly towards affordable housing investments, as well as equitable development and Green New Deal projects, but Strauss himself sponsored the legislation in 2024 to change the spending plan to make permanent large transfusions of JumpStart dollars to the General Fund.
Strauss also chose not to make a 2027 contribution to his own Jumpstart Stabilization Fund in order to gain another $19.1 million, leaving the fund at its minimum required level of $20 million.

“Last year I passed a law that I sponsored regarding the Jumpstart reserves and how they are funded,” Strauss said at the council meeting about his balancing package. “We are suspending the payment for next year, but we're not taking from the Jumpstart reserve, and we're just not adding to it. And colleagues, as you may remember, in the revenue forecast this year, we had a very flat-lined economy. It wasn't going up. It wasn't going down. In the past, it's been going up. This is what reserve accounts are for. When the economy is going down, we need to use them. When the economy is going up, we need to add to them.”

The Jumpstart reserve is intended to provide some security given the high potential volatility of the revenue collected by the Jumpstart tax, which is tied heavily to stock market performance. For a tax that is forecast to collect over $400 million in 2027, a $20 million reserve won’t be very effective at protecting the City’s budget on the downside.

“The Mayor’s Proposed Budget preserves the City’s General Fund fiscal reserves and makes required contributions to the City’s Revenue Stabilization Account (Rainy Day Fund), Emergency Fund, and JumpStart Payroll Expense Tax Reserve,” said Tara Lee, a spokesperson for the Mayor’s Office. “This was an important part of ‘stabilizing the ship’ as we continue to see so much uncertainty in local and national economic conditions that impact City revenues.”
While Strauss is proposing pausing contributions to the Jumpstart reserve, he is not touching the Rainy Day Fund or Emergency Fund.

Strauss also gained an additional $22 million from reducing contributions to the Firefighters Pension Fund Rate Stabilization Reserve, and he will be taking Seattle’s share from the 0.01% Family and Children sales tax increase passed by the King County Council in October. King County will potentially spend the new revenue on expanded shelter and services for homeless families and children, but if Seattle opts into the new taxing authority as Strauss is proposing, the County will collect significantly less. The City of Seattle, on the other hand, will have an additional $7.6 million to program in this budget biennium.

“I correctly identified that the mayor's proposed budget unnecessarily took austere measures to balance the budget, and part of why I said that is there was no new funding of any kind,” Strauss said. “We were able to utilize the sales tax increase that was already passed by King County. We've added new revenue into this chair's package.”

The only way Strauss was able to achieve adding so many councilmember priorities to his balance package, however, was to make most additions one-time adds to the budget, as opposed to ongoing, which threatens the future sustainability of Seattle’s budget.

“When the Mayor put out her budget proposal in September, she made some difficult, disciplined choices needed to make progress toward closing a structural General Fund deficit inherited from prior administrations, while protecting and expanding vital services,” Lee said. “Mayor Wilson has maintained that the budget should be balanced and not rely on one-time funding as that would make the funding issues more difficult down the road.”

Wilson faced a $175 million deficit when preparing her budget proposal for 2027. Councilmember Dionne Foster proposed two pieces of legislation as part of this year’s budget season that would seek to break the deficit cycle Seattle has been enduring for the past several years.

One piece of legislation would require that the Mayor deliver a proposed budget that is balanced in future years, not just the applicable biennium, extending a requirement passed last year that was only for a single year. The other piece of legislation would impose the same requirement on the council.

“We've asked the Mayor to make really difficult decisions to balance the budget this year and in the out years. Let's make sure that we have continuity in our planning,” Foster told The Urbanist . “And for me, it's hard to imagine having that continuity if we have one standard for the Mayor, and we don't also have the same standard for the council. So what I proposed was two different pieces of legislation that required not just the balanced budget for the two years as required by law, but a balanced financial plan in the out years for both branches of government.”
Councilmember Bob Kettle proposed an identical piece of legislation requiring the Mayor to submit a budget plan balanced in future years, and the proposal has enjoyed strong council support.

However, Kettle declined to co-sponsor Foster’s legislation imposing that same good governance requirement on the council. In committee, this bill only received support from Councilmembers Debora Juarez, Eddie Lin, and Alexis Mercedes Rinck.

“I think this is a real opportunity for us to put forward two complementary good governance reforms,” Foster said at the budget meeting. “I think these two pieces of legislation go hand in hand. They strengthen transparency, establish consistent expectations, and help prevent future residents and current residents from service disruptions.”

Foster explained to The Urbanist that one-time funding to community organizations can make it difficult for them to do future planning, including making decisions about whether to hire new staff members. Meanwhile, not practicing budgetary restraint by making investments that need to be ongoing but aren’t balanced in the out years has led to continuing budgetary issues for the City.
Wilson supports both pieces of Foster’s legislation.

“The Mayor supports a requirement for the City – both branches – to present and adopt budgets that balance not just in the next year but for years to come so we can protect the services and programs that our community depends on,” Lee said.

Public safety as a whole made out fairly well in Strauss’s balancing package. The Seattle City Attorney’s Office received more than $1.5 million to help deal with their case backlog , hire two more assistant prosecutors, and pay for more toxicology testing in 2027. The Community Assisted Response and Engagement (CARE) department’s budget was expanded by $253,000 in 2027 (sponsor Councilmember Maritza Rivera) for two more 911 dispatchers for non-emergency calls. The Seattle Fire Department (SFD) is receiving $8.1 million for overtime and more repairs on one of their fire boats.

The Seattle Police Department (SPD) is receiving $870,000 for a position for diversity, equity, and inclusion work and the effort to hire more women officers, noise barriers at their firing range, and several civilian investigation support positions that weren’t previously filled. The council is also trying out some revenue-backed incentives to hire more parking enforcement officers.

However, Kettle did not receive his request for more funding for hiring police officers, which would have cost an additional $792,000 in 2027 and $11.6 million in 2028 (ongoing expenses). If Kettle wants to continue his officer hiring spree, he will be forced to propose his own cuts to pay for it.

Both the Human Services Department (HSD) and the Office of Arts and Culture (ARTS) received substantial further investment in 2027 in Strauss’s package, with more than $10 million being invested in HSD and almost $5 million in ARTS funding.

The HSD funding included $2.5 million in 2026 and $2.5 million in 2027 for Rinck’s “Seattle Stand With Survivors, Every Step” campaign seeking more investment to support survivors of gender-based violence . Rinck had wanted ongoing funding for these services as opposed to funding for two years (and $8 million in investment over two years rather than $5 million), but this is a first step.

Also included in the HSD funding is Foster’s request for $350,000 in 2027 for medical debt relief for Seattle residents, a creative way to assist folks on a local level who are impacted by the health care subsidy Apple Health cuts at the federal level. The City will be partnering with non-profit Undue Medical Debt for this program.

Foster told The Urbanist this partnership will result in clearing at least $6 million of Seattleites’ medical debt. According to her calculations, District 1 currently has the most medical debt held by Undue Medical Debt, amounting to just over $2 million.
“We can make this relatively modest investment in order to wipe out a really significant amount of medical debt in Seattle,” Foster said.

After the already identified $6 million of medical debt, Undue Medical Debt will look to identify additional debt up to the amount specified in the contract with the City, a strategy that has been very effective in other cities. For example, in Memphis, the City spent $159,000 and eventually erased $17 million in resident medical debt, and Kalamazoo spent $100,000 to erase $18 million of medical debt.
The program is low burden for the people who are helped because they don’t have to apply to be helped or go through any kind of administrative process.

“You can work super hard. You can have health insurance; you can do everything that you're supposed to do and have one medical emergency and suddenly be saddled with a ton of financial hardship, right?” Foster said. “I feel like this impacts people's ability to save. It impacts their ability to pay for daily expenses. So I see this as lessening the burden on people deciding: Will I pay my medical bill or will I pay my light bill? Will I start paying down my medical debt or will I pay for my kids' childcare or a new pair of shoes? I think that's going to be really a felt experience for people, and I'm looking forward to people getting that mail and saying your medical debt has been erased.”

Councilmember Rob Saka had his re quest for more funds for the District Project Fund , with Strauss including $1 million per district for transportation projects in 2027. Foster received an additional $5 million for the Office of Housing. And Rivera sponsored the $7.1 million overtime add for SFD.

Possibly the biggest council member winner in terms of investments, aside from Strauss himself, is Council President Joy Hollingsworth. While Hollingsworth didn’t have quite as much money invested into her amendments as a few of her colleagues, both Rivera and Saka had large proposals that either had unanimous backing or directly benefited the majority of their colleagues. Hollingsworth received almost as many new dollars across a larger number of amendments.

Councilmembers spent several hours listening to public comment on the budget proposal on Thursday, and any new amendments, which must be self-balancing, are due on Monday. Votes on those amendments begin on Friday, November 13, with a final vote on the budget scheduled a week later on November 20.
In addition to the City’s expenditures, councilmembers will also be voting on legislation, including Foster’s two budget sustainability measures.

“If you care about financial sustainability, if you care about ensuring that we are budgeting for people in a way that is consistent, I think that you should vote for both of these bills,” Foster said. “I think we just can't grandstand about the budget if we don't want to hold ourselves accountable.”

articles.title: Friday Roundtable: Historic Transit Investments in Puget Sound
articles.author: Michael Smith
paras: The past 5 days may have been the most consequential week for transit in Puget Sound this year. Across the region, voters and elected officials decided to invest in transit for years and decades to come.

On Tuesday, voters in Seattle approved the Seattle Transit Measure (STM) with an overwhelming 72% supporting the measure. The 0.3% sales tax increase will take effect on April 1, 2027 and fund 280,000 bus trips in Seattle each year for 10 years. The measure also funds 22,000 free ORCA cards for low-income, elderly, and families with young children, maintain support for Seattle’s streetcar lines, fund spot improvements to keep buses moving, and help expedite permits and inspections for Link expansion projects in Seattle. The additional bus trips will help grow Seattle’s Very Frequent Transit Network .

In Pierce County, 58% of voters approved a significant expansion to Pierce Transit on Tuesday. The approved proposition increases the sales and use tax within the Pierce County Public Transportation Benefit Area by 0.3%. With this additional funding, Piece Transit will add four new routes, upgrade existing routes 1, 2, and 3 to Stream lines, run most routes until 10pm (8pm on Sunday), and double weekend frequencies from 1hr to 30min on 15 routes. Pierce Transit will also add seasonal and special event service when needed and expand paratransit services. The additional funding will support free fares for seniors aged 65+. Free fares for seniors will start on April 1, 2027. The new routes and other changes will be rolled out in phases to allow time for planning, hiring additional staff, and buying new buses.

On Wednesday, the Everett City Council voted unanimously voted to approve the merger of Everett Transit and Community Transit. The Community Transit Board voted to approve the merger the following day. With these votes, Everett Transit end operations on March 31, 2027. Beginning April 1, Community Transit will operate all current Everett Transit routes and CT is required to maintain or exceed the existing level of service during the transition. Over the four years following the merger, Community Transit will increase service hours in Everett by 50%. In addition, CT will add a new Zip microtransit zone in Everett by March 2028.

To fund the additional service, Community Transit’s 1.2% sales tax will replace Everett’s existing 0.6% sales tax on April 1, 2027. Fares on existing Everett Transit routes will remain at $2 until at least April 2028. Any changes to the fares will require approval from the Community Transit Board.

Community Transit will pay Everett $54.5 million for the existing transit infrastructure and to mitigate any transition costs to the City. Separately, Everett will transfer $16 million in existing transit capital reserves to support replacing buses and other equipment.

Within the past week, voters in Seattle and Pierce County and elected officials in Snohomish County decided to invest in transit. The service improvements across the region will make traveling easier and more convenient for hundreds of thousands of people everyday. As Everett and Tacoma prepare for their respective Link extensions, the decisions made this week will ensure each Link extension connects with a robust bus network.

paras: “Where should I eat in Seattle?” Whether you’re a first-time visitor or a lifer, that question is seemingly simple but the answers are infinitely complex. Some of the main factors to consider are the type of food, price point, neighborhood, and occasion. That’s why Eater’s map of the 38 best restaurants in Seattle exists. This curated list of suggestions attempts to capture the diversity of the food scene in the Seattle metro area, from English pubs serving cumin-y lamb neck meat pies to Indian street food takeout spots, from classic French bistros to modern sushi bars, and so much more. Every place on the list has been open for at least six months, proving its merit.

Like many menus, this map updates every quarter — removal from the Eater 38 doesn’t mean a restaurant isn’t still awesome and won’t return in the future. New to the map as of October 2026: tamale and specialty coffee haven Cafetal Quilombo Cafe, Thai dumpling hotspot E-Jae Pak Mor, and Dim Sum King, which reigns supreme in counter-service dim sum.

But the truth is that the U District is one of the city’s essential dining destinations, with a dizzying array of global cuisines concentrated on its main street, University Way (confusingly known as the Ave).

There’s Korean food, regional Chinese specialties, Indian groceries, Vietnamese kitchens, falafel windows, and more on nearly every block. articles.title: Cafe Lolo Is the Neighborhood Restaurant Every Neighborhood Deserves
articles.author: <name>Kat Thompson</name>
paras: If I were to describe the perfect neighborhood restaurant, Cafe Lolo would completely fit my definition. The food is comforting and nourishing, emphasizing local ingredients, which playfully come together in a way that feels both fresh and familiar. The space is draped in natural light that’s assisted by over a dozen lamps. The inviting dining room is covered in quirky Renaissance-inspired murals that don’t feel disruptive. There are to-go meal kits available for purchase, as well as local beers. It’s an atmosphere that invites you to unwind with a bottle of wine. Owners Leah Engel, Alex Halmi, and Brett Bankson are present, not only flitting about the room, but also cooking the dishes in the kitchen and laughing with customers. If I lived in the neighborhood, just off the main drag of Capitol Hill, it’s somewhere I’d want to return to over and over again.

Cafe Lolo has an extensive wine menu and many local beers, as well as bottles in the fridge you can pick up to-go. Although yes, the wine list — which includes just one glass from Washington, and more options from Oregon and Europe) — is worth perusing, the nonalcoholic tisanes are also made from seasonal ingredients. The strawberry rhubarb soda I had on my visit was effervescent and floral without an overpowering sweetness.

Like the rest of the menu, dessert will change pending seasons — but don’t skip it. My visit included a celebration of ripe, macerated strawberries over a semolina olive oil cake, which had a buttery crust and a tender interior crumb. There was also a scoop of rhubarb sorbet; light, sweet, and sharp.

articles.title: The Best Restaurants in Ballard
articles.author: <name>Mark DeJoy</name>
paras: Once a quiet working-class Nordic-American neighborhood, Ballard is now a nightlife, shopping, and restaurant destination. Boutiques and cocktail bars line Ballard Avenue (home to one of Seattle’s few year-round farmers markets ), and townhomes and high-rises have taken the place of single-family homes. Some of the best restaurants and bars in the city can be found here, along with almost (almost!) too many breweries , which is why if you walk far enough inland you can literally smell the hops. Where else in Seattle can you find Detroit-style pizza, Sri Lankan cocktails, and a congee specialist?
